SECTION 01: CURRICULUM OVERVIEW & ARCHITECTURE MAP

# System Design for Program Managers: The Architectural Handbook

A book-grade reference guide and curriculum designed specifically for **Technical Program Managers (TPMs)**, **Product Managers (PMs)**, and **Engineering Leaders**.

Most system design resources are written by software engineers for software engineers: they dive into byte-level memory layouts, local thread locking, and programming language syntax. This handbook bridges that gap by focusing on what Program Managers are evaluated on in architectural reviews and interviews: **architectural breadth, trade-off analysis, high availability, cross-functional risk mitigation, capacity planning, and program execution roadmaps**.

---

## Repository Governance & Verification

- **Audit Findings**: [AUDIT_REPORT.md](./AUDIT_REPORT.md) (prioritized review of all calculations, claims, and diagrams)
- **Engineering Roadmap**: [IMPROVEMENT_ROADMAP.md](./IMPROVEMENT_ROADMAP.md) (workstream execution plan and acceptance criteria)
- **Architectural Glossary**: [GLOSSARY.md](./GLOSSARY.md) (standardized terms, formulas, and acronyms)
- **Changelog**: [CHANGELOG.md](./CHANGELOG.md) (record of technical revisions and updates)

---

## 1. The Core Philosophy: SWE vs TPM System Design

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph SWE [Software Engineer Focus]
        direction TB
        S1[Code-level data structures]
        S2[Concurrency primitives & mutex locks]
        S3[Algorithm time/space complexity]
        S4[Component-level implementation details]
    end

    subgraph TPM [Program Manager Focus]
        direction TB
        T1[Cross-system boundaries & data contracts]
        T2[Capacity planning & infrastructure cost]
        T3[Single points of failure & disaster recovery]
        T4[Cross-team dependencies & migration roadmaps]
    end

    classDef sweStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef tpmStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class SWE sweStyle;
    class TPM tpmStyle;
```

## 2. Master Table of Contents & Learning Progression

### [Module 1: Distributed Systems Foundations](./01-foundations/README.md)
*Level: Beginner to Intermediate | Prerequisites: Basic networking and client-server concepts*
- **[1.1 Client-Server Networking and Protocols](./01-foundations/01-client-server-networking.md)**  
  TCP vs UDP, HTTP/1.1 through HTTP/3 (QUIC), REST vs gRPC vs WebSockets vs SSE, DNS resolution mechanics, and Content Delivery Networks (CDNs).
- **[1.2 Load Balancing and API Gateways](./01-foundations/02-load-balancing-gateways.md)**  
  Layer 4 vs Layer 7 load balancing, distribution algorithms, Active-Passive vs Active-Active topologies, reverse proxies, and API gateway policy offloading.
- **[1.3 Distributed Caching Strategies](./01-foundations/03-caching-strategies.md)**  
  Multi-tier caching, Cache-Aside vs Write-Through vs Write-Behind, eviction policies (LRU, LFU), Redis vs Memcached, and mitigation for Cache Stampede, Avalanche, and Penetration.

### [Module 2: Data Architecture and Storage](./02-data-architecture/README.md)
*Level: Intermediate | Prerequisites: Module 1, basic SQL understanding*
- **[2.1 Databases: Relational vs NoSQL vs NewSQL](./02-data-architecture/01-databases-sql-vs-nosql.md)**  
  ACID vs BASE, RDBMS vs Document vs Key-Value vs Wide-Column vs Graph, storage engine internals (B-Trees vs LSM-Trees), index penalties, and polyglot persistence.
- **[2.2 Replication, Sharding, and Consistent Hashing](./02-data-architecture/02-sharding-replication.md)**  
  Single-leader vs multi-leader vs leaderless replication, replication lag consistency patterns, horizontal sharding strategies, and consistent hashing rings with virtual nodes.
- **[2.3 The CAP and PACELC Theorems](./02-data-architecture/03-cap-pacelc-theorems.md)**  
  Why network partitions are unavoidable, CP vs AP trade-offs, the PACELC latency dimension, and matching business domains to distributed consistency models.
- **[2.4 Asynchronous Messaging and Event Streaming](./02-data-architecture/04-message-queues-streaming.md)**  
  Message queues (RabbitMQ, SQS) vs event streaming (Kafka, Kinesis), delivery semantics (at-least-once + idempotency), Dead Letter Queues (DLQ), and partition consumer groups.

### [Module 3: System Resilience, Scale, and NFRs](./03-system-resilience-scale/README.md)
*Level: Intermediate to Advanced | Prerequisites: Modules 1 and 2*
- **[3.1 Architectural Scalability Patterns](./03-system-resilience-scale/01-scalability-patterns.md)**  
  Vertical vs horizontal scale limits, externalizing state to create stateless application fleets, CQRS read/write segregation, and auto-scaling cooldown policies.
- **[3.2 Fault Tolerance, Resilience, and Rate Limiting](./03-system-resilience-scale/02-fault-tolerance-patterns.md)**  
  Cascading failures, Circuit Breaker state machines, exponential backoff with full jitter, rate limiting algorithms (Token Bucket, Sliding Window), bulkheads, and idempotency keys.
- **[3.3 High Availability, NFRs, and Disaster Recovery](./03-system-resilience-scale/03-slas-slis-slos-nfrs.md)**  
  The SLI/SLO/SLA hierarchy, High Availability math ("The Nines"), error budgets, RPO and RTO metrics, and the disaster recovery continuum from Backup to Multi-Region Active-Active.

### [Module 4: The TPM Execution and Architecture Framework](./04-tpm-execution-framework/README.md)
*Level: Advanced / Leadership | Prerequisites: Modules 1, 2, and 3*
- **[4.1 The TPM System Design Framework](./04-tpm-execution-framework/01-tpm-system-design-framework.md)**  
  The 5-stage blueprint for 45-minute interviews and design reviews, time management techniques, and common anti-patterns to avoid.
- **[4.2 Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Planning](./04-tpm-execution-framework/02-back-of-the-envelope-math.md)**  
  Powers-of-two reference table, latency numbers every TPM should know, and formulas for calculating QPS, storage growth, network bandwidth, and memory sizing.
- **[4.3 Migration and Safe Deployment Strategies](./04-tpm-execution-framework/03-migration-deployment-strategies.md)**  
  The Strangler Fig pattern for monolith decommissioning, Rolling vs Blue-Green vs Canary deployments, Shadow Traffic (Dark Launching), feature flags, and automated rollback criteria.
- **[4.4 Observability, Security, and Governance](./04-tpm-execution-framework/04-observability-governance.md)**  
  Metrics vs Logs vs Distributed Tracing (OpenTelemetry), Google SRE Four Golden Signals, AuthN vs AuthZ (OAuth2, OIDC, JWT), envelope encryption, and regulatory compliance (GDPR, SOC 2).

### [Module 5: Real-World Architecture Case Studies](./05-real-world-case-studies/README.md)
*Level: Comprehensive Synthesis | Prerequisites: All preceding modules*
- **[5.1 Designing a Global URL Shortener (TinyURL / Bitly)](./05-real-world-case-studies/01-url-shortener.md)**  
  Key Generation Service (KGS), Base62 hashing, HTTP 301 vs 302 analytics trade-offs, DynamoDB partitioning, and caching tiers.
- **[5.2 Scalable Multi-Channel Notification Engine](./05-real-world-case-studies/02-notification-engine.md)**  
  Multi-channel dispatch (Push, SMS, Email), priority queues (OTP vs Marketing), quiet-hour evaluation, vendor circuit breakers, and SMS cost routing cascades.
- **[5.3 Global Video Streaming Platform (YouTube / Netflix)](./05-real-world-case-studies/03-video-streaming-platform.md)**  
  Chunk-based DAG video transcoding, Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (HLS / MPEG-DASH), multi-terabit bandwidth cost management, and ISP edge caching appliances.
- **[5.4 Real-Time Ride-Sharing Dispatch (Uber / Lyft)](./05-real-world-case-studies/04-ride-sharing-dispatch.md)**  
  1.25M location writes/sec, Uber H3 hexagonal spatial indexing, distributed driver locking, WebSocket lifecycle management, and trip state machines.
- **[5.5 High-Concurrency Flash Sale and Distributed Checkout](./05-real-world-case-studies/05-distributed-ecommerce-checkout.md)**  
  Atomic in-memory inventory reservation (Redis Lua scripts), the Saga orchestration pattern with compensating transactions, payment idempotency, and virtual waiting rooms.

---

## 5. TPM System Design Evaluation Rubric

Top technology companies assess TPM candidates across five primary dimensions:

| Evaluation Dimension | Expectations for Senior TPM |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1. Requirements & Scope Clarification** | Asks targeted questions to bound scope; separates functional from non-functional requirements; calculates quantitative scale targets (QPS, storage, bandwidth). |
| **2. Architectural Breadth & Component Selection** | Selects appropriate building blocks (load balancers, gateways, databases, caches, queues); justifies choices using technical and business trade-offs. |
| **3. Scalability & Resilience Depth** | Identifies single points of failure (SPOFs); designs for graceful degradation; applies rate limiting, circuit breakers, and consistent hashing. |
| **4. Data Modeling & Storage Strategy** | Chooses relational vs NoSQL vs NewSQL based on read/write patterns; designs partition keys; plans for replication lag and consistency models. |
| **5. Program Execution & Governance Lens** | Identifies cross-team dependencies; defines zero-downtime migration strategies (Strangler Fig, Canary); estimates cloud costs; defines rollback SLI triggers. |

---

Contributions, corrections, and additional case studies from practicing TPMs and engineering leaders are welcome. Please open a pull request or issue following the standard GitHub markdown guidelines and style conventions.

SECTION 02: MASTER ARCHITECTURAL GLOSSARY
FILE: GLOSSARY.md

# Distributed Systems Glossary for Program Managers

[Home](./README.md) > **Architectural Glossary**

This glossary defines foundational distributed systems, cloud infrastructure, and technical program governance terminology. Every Technical Program Manager should understand these definitions, formulas, and architectural trade-offs.

---

## A

### ACID
A set of properties guaranteeing that database transactions are processed reliably:
- **Atomicity**: All operations in a transaction succeed, or the entire transaction is rolled back.
- **Consistency**: Data written to the database satisfies all defined schema constraints, cascades, and triggers.
- **Isolation**: Concurrent transactions execute without cross-contaminating each other.
- **Durability**: Once committed, transaction data survives power loss, system crashes, and reboots via write-ahead logging (WAL).

### Active-Active vs Active-Passive
- **Active-Active**: Redundant compute and database nodes simultaneously receive and process live production traffic, maximizing infrastructure utilization.
- **Active-Passive**: Traffic routes exclusively to a primary instance; a standby replica remains idle until a failure triggers failover via heartbeat protocols (e.g. VRRP).

### Architectural Decision Record (ADR)
A lightweight document capturing a significant technical choice, including its context, alternatives considered, decision outcome, and long-term consequences.

---

## B

### Backpressure
A flow-control mechanism where a downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to slow down or pause message transmission when buffer capacity approaches saturation.

### BASE
The philosophical counterpoint to ACID in distributed NoSQL databases:
- **Basically Available**: The system guarantees availability by continuing to operate despite node partitions.
- **Soft State**: System data may drift or change over time without explicit user input due to eventual consistency.
- **Eventual Consistency**: Replicas will converge to identical values given sufficient time without new writes.

### Bloom Filter
A space-efficient, probabilistic data structure used to test set membership. A Bloom filter can return false positives (saying an item exists when it does not), but **never returns false negatives** (if it says an item does not exist, it definitely does not exist). Frequently placed in front of caches to prevent Cache Penetration.

### Bulkhead Pattern
An architectural isolation pattern named after watertight compartments in ships. By segregating thread pools, connection limits, and memory quotas across services, a failure in one non-critical component (e.g. PDF generation) cannot exhaust resources required for critical paths (e.g. user authentication).

---

## C

### Cache Avalanche
A catastrophic failure mode occurring when hundreds of thousands of cache keys expire simultaneously, causing the entire incoming traffic volume to hit downstream databases. Mitigated by adding randomized jitter to TTL expirations.

### Cache Penetration
An anti-pattern where clients repeatedly query non-existent keys (e.g. negative IDs). Cache misses force repeated database reads. Mitigated by Bloom filters or caching null results with short TTLs.

### Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd)
A sudden wave of concurrent cache misses occurring when a viral or heavily accessed key expires, causing thousands of application threads to query the primary database for the exact same record at the same millisecond. Mitigated by distributed mutex locking or probabilistic early regeneration (XFetch).

### Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
A caching pattern where the application code directly coordinates between cache and database: querying cache first, reading database on miss, and populating cache before returning.

### CAP Theorem
Formulated by Eric Brewer and proved by Gilbert and Lynch: a distributed data store can guarantee at most two out of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance simultaneously. In real-world physical networks, partitions ($P$) are inevitable; systems must choose between Consistency ($CP$) or Availability ($AP$).

### Change Data Capture (CDC)
A software design pattern that monitors and captures committed row-level changes from a database transaction log (e.g. Debezium reading MySQL binlog) and streams them to message brokers like Kafka.

### Circuit Breaker Pattern
A stability pattern that prevents an application from repeatedly attempting an operation that is failing. Transitions across three states: **Closed** (normal execution), **Open** (failing fast immediately without network calls), and **Half-Open** (allowing canary probe requests to verify downstream recovery).

### Consistent Hashing
A distributed hashing technique mapping nodes and keys onto a circular hash ring ($0$ to $2^{32}-1$). When servers are added or removed, only $K/N$ keys need to be rebalanced (where $K$ is total keys, $N$ is server count). Uses virtual nodes (vnodes) to achieve uniform distribution and prevent hot spots.

### CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
An architectural pattern that separates mutation operations (Commands: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`) from read operations (Queries: `SELECT`) into independent models and databases.

---

## D

### Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)
A specialized message queue dedicated to storing malformed messages or poison pills that have exceeded retry thresholds, preventing them from blocking consumer progress.

### Distributed Tracing
A diagnostic methodology tracking the end-to-end path of an execution across multiple microservices by injecting a unique **Trace ID** and propagating it through HTTP headers (W3C `traceparent`).

---

## E

### Error Budget
The maximum permissible unreliability of a service over a rolling window (typically 30 days):
$$\text{Error Budget} = 100\% - \text{SLO}$$
When an error budget is exhausted, product feature deployments freeze until reliability engineering remediates the root cause.

### Exponential Backoff with Jitter
A retry algorithm where clients progressively double wait duration between retries, adding randomized noise (jitter) to prevent synchronized waves of traffic (retry storms).

---

## H

### H3 Spatial Index
An open-source hexagonal hierarchical spatial indexing system developed by Uber. Partitions the Earth into hexagonal cells where all 6 neighboring cells are equidistant, eliminating corner distortions found in square grids (Geohashes).

### High Availability ("The Nines")
A metric quantifying the proportion of time a system is operational. Calculated as:
$$\text{Availability} = \frac{\text{Uptime}}{\text{Uptime} + \text{Downtime}} \times 100\%$$
- **99.9% (Three Nines)**: 8.76 hours downtime/year.
- **99.99% (Four Nines)**: 52.6 minutes downtime/year.
- **99.999% (Five Nines)**: 5.26 minutes downtime/year.

---

## I

### Idempotency
A mathematical property where executing an operation multiple times produces the exact same outcome as executing it once:
$$f(f(x)) = f(x)$$
In distributed systems, mutation APIs pass an **Idempotency Key** to ensure network retries do not duplicate state changes (e.g. double-charging a credit card).

---

## L

### Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing
- **Layer 4**: Operates at the transport layer (TCP/UDP). Routes traffic based on source/destination IP addresses and ports without inspecting application payloads. Ultra-fast, minimal CPU overhead.
- **Layer 7**: Operates at the application layer (HTTP/HTTPS). Inspects URIs, HTTP headers, cookies, and payloads. Enables path-based routing, TLS termination, and canary traffic splitting.

### LSM-Tree (Log-Structured Merge-Tree)
A write-optimized storage engine (used in Cassandra, RocksDB) that appends writes sequentially to an in-memory MemTable and write-ahead log (WAL), later flushing them sequentially to immutable SSTables on disk. Trades read latency for extreme write throughput.

---

## O

### OpenTelemetry (OTel)
A vendor-neutral, open-source observability framework under the CNCF providing standardized APIs, libraries, and agents to collect metrics, logs, and distributed traces.

---

## P

### PACELC Theorem
An extension of the CAP theorem by Daniel Abadi addressing normal operating conditions:
$$\text{If } \mathbf{P} \text{ (Partition): Choose } \mathbf{A} \text{ or } \mathbf{C}; \quad \text{EL} \text{se: Choose } \mathbf{L} \text{ (Latency) or } \mathbf{C} \text{ (Consistency)}$$

### Poison Pill
A malformed message payload (e.g. invalid syntax) that causes consumer applications to crash on every processing attempt. Handled via Dead Letter Queues (DLQ).

---

## R

### Rate Limiting
A defensive traffic-shaping technique restricting incoming request volume per client. Common algorithms include **Token Bucket** (allows controlled bursts), **Leaky Bucket** (smooths traffic to a constant rate), and **Sliding Window Counter** (approximates rolling windows).

### Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
The maximum acceptable duration of data loss measured backward in time from a disaster event (e.g. RPO of 15 minutes means at most 15 minutes of uncommitted transactional data can be lost).

### Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
The maximum acceptable duration of downtime required to restore normal system operations following an outage (e.g. RTO of 1 hour means secondary infrastructure must be fully serving traffic within 60 minutes).

---

## S

### Saga Pattern
A distributed transaction pattern coordinating multiple local transactions across microservices without distributed two-phase locking. If a downstream step fails, the Saga orchestrator executes **compensating transactions** to roll back preceding steps in reverse order.

### SLA vs SLO vs SLI
- **SLI (Service Level Indicator)**: A quantifiable metric tracking service health in real time (e.g. percentage of successful requests under 200ms).
- **SLO (Service Level Objective)**: The internal engineering target agreed upon by Product, TPM, and Engineering (e.g. 99.9% of requests meet SLI over 30 days).
- **SLA (Service Level Agreement)**: The contractual promise to customers with financial penalties (service credits) if breached.

### Strangler Fig Pattern
An incremental legacy migration strategy where an API Gateway or facade proxy intercepts incoming traffic, gradually routing specific service paths to new microservices until the legacy monolith can be safely decommissioned.

---

## W

### WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events (SSE)
- **WebSockets**: Full-duplex, bidirectional communication over a single persistent TCP socket. Ideal for chat, gaming, and collaborative editing.
- **Server-Sent Events (SSE)**: Unidirectional streaming from server to client over standard HTTP. Ideal for live dashboards, stock tickers, and LLM text generation.

# Module 1: Distributed Systems Foundations

[Home](../README.md) > **Module 1: Foundations**

---

## Overview

Modern distributed systems power internet-scale applications by coordinating hundreds of independent services across global networks. This module provides the foundational building blocks required for Technical Program Managers: network transport protocols, application layer APIs, ingress routing, and multi-tier caching architectures.

---

## Module Learning Objectives

1. **Protocol Selection**: Learn how to evaluate trade-offs between TCP, UDP, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 (QUIC) based on latency SLAs and network conditions.
2. **API Styles**: Master the criteria for selecting REST, gRPC, GraphQL, WebSockets, or Server-Sent Events for internal and external interfaces.
3. **Ingress Architecture**: Understand how DNS, CDNs, Layer 4/Layer 7 load balancers, and API Gateways collaborate to route client requests securely and reliably.
4. **Caching Strategies**: Evaluate multi-tier caching patterns (Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Write-Behind) and prevent production incidents like Cache Stampedes and Avalanches.

---

## Chapter Directory

| Chapter | Title | Focus Areas | Key Trade-offs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **[1.1](./01-client-server-networking.md)** | Client-Server Networking & Protocols | TCP/UDP, HTTP evolution, REST, gRPC, WebSockets, DNS, CDNs | Head-of-line blocking, binary multiplexing, connection migration |
| **[1.2](./02-load-balancing-gateways.md)** | Load Balancing & API Gateways | L4 vs L7 routing, Active-Active, reverse proxies, API Gateway offload | Throughput vs deep packet inspection, SPOF mitigation |
| **[1.3](./03-caching-strategies.md)** | Distributed Caching Strategies | Multi-tier cache, read/write patterns, eviction (LRU/LFU), Redis | Consistency vs latency, stampede mitigation, working set sizing |

---

## Suggested Prerequisites

- Understanding of client-server request/response cycles.
- Basic familiarity with IP addressing and ports.
- Foundational knowledge of web browsers and mobile application clients.

SECTION 04: MODULE 1 CHAPTER 1: CLIENT-SERVER NETWORKING & PROTOCOLS

# Module 1.1: Client-Server Networking and Communication Protocols

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 1: Foundations](./README.md) > **Chapter 1.1: Networking & Protocols**

---

Communication protocols define how distributed components exchange data, negotiate connections, and maintain reliability. As a Technical Program Manager, choosing the right protocol impacts system latency, infrastructure costs, battery life on mobile devices, and cross-team interface contracts.

---

## 1. Network Protocol Fundamentals

Modern distributed architectures operate across multiple layers of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) and TCP/IP models. Program managers should understand the trade-offs between transport-layer protocols (TCP vs UDP) and application-layer protocols (HTTP, WebSockets, gRPC).

### Transport Layer: TCP vs UDP

| Feature | TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) | UDP (User Datagram Protocol) | Architectural Impact |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Connection Model** | Connection-oriented (3-way handshake) | Connectionless (fire and forget) | TCP adds 1 RTT before data transfer; UDP starts instantly |
| **Reliability** | Guaranteed in-order packet delivery via ACKs and retransmissions | Best effort; packet loss and out-of-order arrival possible | TCP prevents corrupted/missing data; UDP eliminates retransmit latency |
| **Flow & Congestion** | Built-in flow control (sliding window) and congestion avoidance | None at protocol level; must be handled by application | TCP prevents network saturation; UDP streams at arbitrary rates |
| **Header Overhead** | 20 to 60 bytes per packet | 8 bytes per packet | UDP conserves bandwidth and packet processing CPU |
| **Primary Use Cases** | APIs, financial ledgers, transactional databases, file storage | Live video streaming (WebRTC), VoIP, DNS lookups, gaming | Choose TCP for correctness; choose UDP for real-time speed |

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Client as Client Device
    participant Server as Application Server

    Note over Client,Server: TCP 3-Way Handshake (1 RTT overhead before data)
    Client->>Server: SYN (Synchronize sequence number)
    Server->>Client: SYN-ACK (Acknowledge and send sequence number)
    Client->>Server: ACK (Acknowledge)
    Note over Client,Server: Connection Established. Data Exchange Begins.
    Client->>Server: HTTP Request / Payload
    Server->>Client: HTTP Response / Payload
```

---

## 2. Evolution of HTTP: HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/3

Understanding the HTTP evolution helps TPMs evaluate migration programs and justify client infrastructure upgrades.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph H1 [HTTP/1.1 - RFC 7230]
        direction TB
        A1[Single Request per TCP Connection<br/>Pipelining suffers from Head-of-Line blocking<br/>Requires 6 parallel TCP sockets per domain]
    end

    subgraph H2 [HTTP/2 - RFC 7540]
        direction TB
        A2[Single TCP connection per host<br/>Binary framing layer with stream multiplexing<br/>HPACK header compression<br/>TCP-level packet loss stalls all streams]
    end

    subgraph H3 [HTTP/3 - RFC 9114 / QUIC RFC 9000]
        direction TB
        A3[Built on QUIC over UDP<br/>Zero-RTT connection re-establishment<br/>Independent stream loss recovery<br/>Connection migration across Wi-Fi and Cellular]
    end

    H1 -->|Evolved for Multiplexing| H2
    H2 -->|Evolved to Eliminate TCP HOL Blocking| H3

    classDef protoStyle fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class H1,H2,H3 protoStyle;
```

### Protocol Comparison for Engineering Roadmaps

1. **HTTP/1.1**:
   - *Mechanics*: Persistent connections (`Keep-Alive`), chunked transfer encoding.
   - *Limitation*: Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking at application level. Browsers open 6 parallel TCP connections per host to bypass this, multiplying server memory overhead and handshake latency.

2. **HTTP/2**:
   - *Mechanics*: Binary framing layer, multiplexing multiple request/response streams over a single TCP connection, server push, header compression (HPACK).
   - *Limitation*: TCP-level HoL blocking. Because TCP enforces strict packet order, if a single packet drops on a flaky mobile connection, all multiplexed HTTP/2 streams stall until TCP retransmits the missing segment.

3. **HTTP/3 (QUIC)**:
   - *Mechanics*: Runs over UDP instead of TCP. QUIC moves stream management into the transport layer. Packet loss on Stream A does not pause Stream B.
   - *TPM Business Impact*: 0-RTT connection resumption accelerates page load times for returning mobile users; **Connection Migration** allows mobile users to transition from home Wi-Fi to cellular data without dropping active streams or re-authenticating.

---

## 3. Communication Styles: API Decision Framework

Different program initiatives require distinct API paradigms. Below is the decision framework for technical program managers:

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start[What is the primary communication requirement?] --> Q1{Real-time, bidirectional, or high frequency?}
    
    Q1 -->|Yes| Q2{Need server to push updates only?}
    Q2 -->|Yes| SSE[Server-Sent Events: Dashboards, Stock Tickers]
    Q2 -->|No| WS[WebSockets: Real-time Chat, Collaborative Docs, Gaming]
    
    Q1 -->|No| Q3{Internal microservices or Public/Partner API?}
    Q3 -->|Internal Microservices| GRPC[gRPC / Protobuf: High throughput, low latency, strict schemas]
    Q3 -->|Public / Partner API| Q4{Complex nested client queries?}
    Q4 -->|Yes| GQL[GraphQL: Client-driven query shapes, mobile bandwidth efficiency]
    Q4 -->|No| REST[REST APIs: Universal standard, easy caching, decoupled]

    classDef decision fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef tech fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:2px;
    class Start,Q1,Q2,Q3,Q4 decision;
    class SSE,WS,GRPC,GQL,REST tech;
```

### Detailed Protocol Evaluation Table

| Pattern | Transport | Data Format | Directionality | Ideal Use Case | Operational Considerations for TPMs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **REST** | HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 | JSON, XML | Request / Response | Public APIs, CRUD microservices | Universal client compatibility, standard edge caching, simple API versioning |
| **gRPC** | HTTP/2, HTTP/3 | Protocol Buffers (Binary) | Bidirectional Streaming & RPC | Low-latency internal microservices | 5x to 10x faster serialization than JSON; requires Protobuf schema governance tooling |
| **GraphQL** | HTTP | JSON | Request / Response | Mobile applications with variable screen layouts | Prevents over/under-fetching; query complexity risks backend database CPU exhaustion |
| **WebSockets** | TCP (Upgraded from HTTP) | Text / Binary | Full-Duplex (Bidirectional) | Chat apps, trading desks, driver location tracking | Stateful connections complicate auto-scaling; requires sticky sessions or socket broker fleets |
| **Server-Sent Events** | HTTP | Text / Event-Stream | Unidirectional (Server to Client) | Live dashboards, notifications, LLM token streaming | Reuses standard HTTP/2 infrastructure; traverses corporate firewalls with zero special proxy configuration |

---

## 4. DNS (Domain Name System) Resolution Mechanics

DNS translates human-readable hostnames (e.g. `api.example.com`) into routable IP addresses. Understanding DNS resolution is critical when managing global deployments, zero-downtime cutovers, and disaster recovery failovers.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Client as User Device
    participant Recur as Recursive Resolver (ISP / 8.8.8.8)
    participant Root as Root DNS Server (.)
    participant TLD as TLD DNS Server (.com)
    participant Auth as Authoritative DNS Server (example.com)

    Client->>Recur: Query: api.example.com
    Note over Recur: Check local cache first. If missed:
    Recur->>Root: Where is .com?
    Root-->>Recur: Referral to .com TLD Nameserver
    Recur->>TLD: Where is example.com?
    TLD-->>Recur: Referral to example.com Authoritative Nameserver
    Recur->>Auth: What is IP for api.example.com?
    Auth-->>Recur: Return IP: 198.51.100.45 (TTL = 300s)
    Recur-->>Client: Return IP: 198.51.100.45
```

### DNS Routing Policies for TPMs

- **Latency-Based Routing**: Directs user traffic to the cloud region with the lowest round-trip network latency.
- **Geolocation Routing**: Directs users based on geographical origin (essential for enforcing European GDPR data residency).
- **Weighted Round-Robin**: Splits traffic proportionately across endpoints (ideal for multi-week canary rollouts).
- **Health Check & Failover Routing**: Automatically diverts DNS queries away from impaired regions when automated synthetic health probes fail.
- **Time-to-Live (TTL) Strategy**:
  - *Migration Phase (Low TTL: 60s)*: Ensures rapid rollback and swift DNS propagation if the new cluster experiences issues.
  - *Steady-State Phase (High TTL: 3600s)*: Maximizes resolver cache hits, reducing lookup latency and DNS hosting costs.

---

## 5. Content Delivery Networks (CDNs)

A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers (Points of Presence, or POPs) that cache content near end users.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    User[End User Device] -->|1. Request Asset /image.png| POP[CDN Edge POP]
    POP -->|2a. Cache Hit: Sub-10ms Response| User
    POP -->|2b. Cache Miss| OriginShield[Origin Shield / Regional Mid-Tier]
    OriginShield -->|3. Fetch from Cloud Origin| Origin[Origin Object Store S3 / Cloud Storage]
    Origin --> OriginShield
    OriginShield --> POP
    POP --> User

    classDef cdnStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class POP,OriginShield cdnStyle;
```

### CDN Capabilities Beyond Static Caching

1. **Static Asset Caching**: Images, CSS, JavaScript bundles, video segments.
2. **Dynamic Site Acceleration (DSA)**: Optimizes route calculation over private cloud backbones, keeping TCP connections pre-warmed between CDN edge POPs and origin servers.
3. **Edge Compute (Workers / Cloudflare Workers / Lambda@Edge)**: Header rewriting, A/B testing splits, authentication validation, and geolocation personalization at the perimeter.
4. **DDoS Protection & Web Application Firewall (WAF)**: Absorbs volumetric Layer 3/4 flood attacks and filters Layer 7 injection attacks (SQLi, XSS) before hitting internal clusters.

### Critical CDN Metrics for Program Reviews

- **Cache Hit Ratio (CHR)**: Target greater than 90% for static media. Formula: $\text{CHR} = \frac{\text{Cache Hits}}{\text{Cache Hits} + \text{Cache Misses}}$.
- **Origin Offload**: Percentage of bandwidth absorbed by the CDN instead of origin servers. Directly reduces cloud egress bandwidth bills.
- **Purge Latency**: Time required to invalidate cached assets globally when deploying breaking client releases.

---

## 6. TPM Review Checklist

When leading architectural discussions on networking and communication:

- [ ] Does the chosen protocol support the required latency and throughput SLAs?
- [ ] Are public-facing endpoints secured behind HTTPS (TLS 1.3) with HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) enabled?
- [ ] For real-time features, did the team evaluate Server-Sent Events before defaulting to stateful WebSockets?
- [ ] What is the planned DNS TTL setting during steady-state versus migration phases?
- [ ] Is CDN caching configured with appropriate `Cache-Control` headers and cache-busting version hashes?
- [ ] Are internal microservices leveraging gRPC with strict Protocol Buffer definitions for schema governance?

---

## 7. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **RFC 9000**: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport (IETF, 2021).
- **RFC 9114**: HTTP/3 (IETF, 2022).
- **RFC 7540**: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2) (IETF, 2015).
- **RFC 6455**: The WebSocket Protocol (IETF, 2011).
- **RFC 1034 & RFC 1035**: Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities (IETF, 1987).
- *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly Media, 2017) - Chapter 1: Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Systems.

SECTION 05: MODULE 1 CHAPTER 2: LOAD BALANCING & API GATEWAYS
FILE: 01-foundations/02-load-balancing-gateways.md

# Module 1.2: Load Balancing and API Gateways

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 1: Foundations](./README.md) > **Chapter 1.2: Load Balancing & API Gateways**

---

Load balancers and API gateways form the front door of modern distributed architectures. They ensure high availability, prevent server saturation, enforce security policies, and route requests efficiently across fleet instances. For technical program managers, these components represent critical single points of failure (SPOFs) and cost drivers.

---

## 1. Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing

Load balancers operate at different layers of the OSI model, trading inspection depth for raw packet throughput.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Client[Incoming Client Traffic] --> L4[Layer 4 Load Balancer: IP + Port Routing]
    
    L4 -->|TCP Stream Passthrough| L7A[Layer 7 Load Balancer / API Gateway]
    L4 -->|TCP Stream Passthrough| L7B[Layer 7 Load Balancer / API Gateway]
    
    L7A -->|Inspect Path /orders| SvcA[Orders Microservice]
    L7A -->|Inspect Path /users| SvcB[Users Microservice]
    L7B -->|Inspect Path /payments| SvcC[Payments Microservice]

    classDef lbStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef svcStyle fill:#f0fdf4,stroke:#16a34a,stroke-width:1px;
    class L4,L7A,L7B lbStyle;
    class SvcA,SvcB,SvcC svcStyle;
```

### Deep-Dive Comparison

| Dimension | Layer 4 (Transport Layer) | Layer 7 (Application Layer) | Architectural Guidance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Routing Criteria** | Source IP, Source Port, Dest IP, Dest Port, TCP/UDP protocol | HTTP URI, HTTP Headers, Cookies, Request Body, Content-Type | L4 for raw protocol speed; L7 for path/header routing |
| **Payload Inspection** | No inspection; forwards raw packets directly | Full inspection; terminates TCP and parses HTTP payload | L7 allows security scanning; L4 preserves end-to-end privacy |
| **Performance** | Ultra-high throughput, sub-millisecond latency, minimal CPU | Higher CPU and memory consumption per request | Size L7 clusters with 3x compute buffer compared to L4 |
| **SSL/TLS Termination** | Passes encrypted packets or decrypts without HTTP inspection | Full SSL/TLS termination and re-encryption to backends | Centralize TLS at L7 to offload CPU from backend pods |
| **Smart Routing** | Cannot route based on URL path or session cookies | Supports canary traffic splitting, path routing, header filtering | Essential for microservice service discovery |
| **Representative Technologies** | AWS NLB (Network Load Balancer), HAProxy (TCP mode), IPVS, Maglev | AWS ALB, NGINX, Envoy Proxy, Traefik, Kong, HAProxy (HTTP mode) | Combine L4 at edge with L7 for microservice ingress |

---

## 2. Load Balancing Algorithms

Choosing the right distribution algorithm directly impacts p99 tail latency and resource utilization.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Algorithms [Load Balancing Algorithms]
        RR[Round Robin / Weighted Round Robin]
        LC[Least Connections / Weighted Least Connections]
        IPH[IP Hash / Source Hash]
        CH[Consistent Hashing]
    end

    RR -->|Best For| U1[Stateless identical backend instances]
    LC -->|Best For| U2[Long-lived connections e.g. WebSockets, heavy compute]
    IPH -->|Best For| U3[Sticky sessions without shared session storage]
    CH -->|Best For| U4[Distributed caching tiers with dynamic nodes]

    classDef algoStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class RR,LC,IPH,CH algoStyle;
```

1. **Round Robin**:
   - Cycles through servers sequentially.
   - *Limitation*: Assumes all servers have identical capacity and all requests require equal processing time. Can cause queue pile-ups on slower instances.
2. **Weighted Round Robin**:
   - Assigns a numeric weight reflecting hardware capacity (e.g. an 8-core node receives 2x the requests of a 4-core node).
3. **Least Connections**:
   - Routes to the server with fewest active concurrent connections. Essential for variable-duration transactions like report generation or video encoding.
4. **Consistent Hashing**:
   - Maps requests and servers to a virtual ring. Minimizes cache misses when backends scale up or down dynamically.

---

## 3. High Availability Topologies: Active-Passive vs Active-Active

High availability eliminates single points of failure at the network ingress layer.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph TopologyAP [Active-Passive Topology]
        direction TB
        ClientAP[DNS / Virtual IP VIP] --> LB_Active[Primary Active LB]
        LB_Active -.->|Heartbeat / Keepalived VRRP| LB_Passive[Standby Passive LB]
        LB_Active --> BackendsAP[Backend Application Pool]
    end

    subgraph TopologyAA [Active-Active Topology with Anycast BGP]
        direction TB
        ClientAA[Global Anycast IP] --> Router[BGP Border Router]
        Router --> LB1[Active LB Node 1]
        Router --> LB2[Active LB Node 2]
        LB1 --> BackendsAA[Backend Application Pool]
        LB2 --> BackendsAA
    end

    classDef topoStyle fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:1px;
    class TopologyAP,TopologyAA topoStyle;
```

### Architectural Trade-offs

- **Active-Passive (Failover via VRRP / Keepalived)**:
  - Simple to implement; standby node consumes idle compute cost.
  - Failover takes 1 to 5 seconds while virtual IP address migrates, which may cause brief connection drops for active TCP streams.
- **Active-Active (BGP Anycast / DNS Multi-A Records)**:
  - Full resource utilization; traffic is load-balanced across all gateways simultaneously.
  - Requires automated health-checking to withdraw BGP routes instantly if a node crashes to avoid routing traffic to a dead host.

---

## 4. The API Gateway Pattern

In a microservice architecture, client applications should never interact directly with hundreds of internal microservices. The API Gateway acts as a unified reverse proxy and policy enforcement point.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Clients[Web / Mobile Clients] -->|HTTPS Requests| GW[API Gateway / Ingress]
    
    subgraph GatewayResponsibilities [Gateway Cross-Cutting Concerns]
        direction TB
        R1[Authentication & Authorization: JWT Verification]
        R2[Rate Limiting & Throttling: Token Bucket]
        R3[SSL / TLS Termination]
        R4[Path Routing & Canary Traffic Splitting]
        R5[Telemetry, Logging & Distributed Tracing]
    end

    GW --- GatewayResponsibilities

    GW -->|gRPC / Internal HTTP| Svc1[Catalog Service]
    GW -->|gRPC / Internal HTTP| Svc2[Payment Service]
    GW -->|gRPC / Internal HTTP| Svc3[Notification Service]

    classDef gwStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px;
    class GW gwStyle;
```

### Core API Gateway Responsibilities

1. **Request Routing & Path Translation**:
   - Routes `/api/v1/checkout` to the Checkout cluster and `/api/v1/search` to the Search cluster.
2. **Security & Authentication Offload**:
   - Validates OAuth2 / OpenID Connect tokens, decodes JWT signatures, and passes verified user claims as internal HTTP headers (`X-User-ID`, `X-User-Role`) to backends.
3. **Rate Limiting & Abuse Prevention**:
   - Enforces tier-based quotas (e.g. 100 requests per minute for free tier, 5000 for enterprise) using Redis-backed token buckets.
4. **SSL/TLS Termination**:
   - Manages certificates centrally, decrypts incoming traffic, and communicates with internal services over high-speed private virtual private clouds (VPCs).
5. **Observability Injection**:
   - Injects correlation IDs (`X-Correlation-ID` or W3C `traceparent`) to enable end-to-end distributed tracing across microservices.

---

## 5. Reverse Proxy vs API Gateway vs Ingress Controller

Technical program managers often hear these terms used interchangeably. Here is the architectural distinction:

| Component | Primary Scope | Typical Technology |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Reverse Proxy** | Handles single-site traffic, static asset serving, compression, basic load balancing | NGINX, Apache, HAProxy |
| **API Gateway** | Rich business-aware API management: rate limiting, auth, mocking, developer portals, monetization | Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway, Envoy |
| **Ingress Controller** | Bridges external traffic into Kubernetes cluster pods based on Ingress resource definitions | NGINX Ingress, Traefik, Istio Gateway |

---

## 6. Health Checks and Failover Mechanics

Load balancers rely on active and passive health checks to detect failing servers and avoid routing user requests to dead nodes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant LB as Load Balancer
    participant S1 as Server 1 (Healthy)
    participant S2 as Server 2 (Failing)

    LB->>S1: GET /healthz
    S1-->>LB: 200 OK (Response time: 15ms)
    LB->>S2: GET /healthz
    Note over S2: Process hanging / Database connection pool dead
    S2-->>LB: 503 Service Unavailable (or Timeout after 2000ms)
    Note over LB: Mark Server 2 Unhealthy after 3 consecutive failures
    LB->>LB: Remove Server 2 from active routing pool
```

### Health Check Strategy Best Practices

- **Shallow Health Check (`/ping`)**: Confirms the web process is running. Fast and lightweight, but does not verify downstream database connectivity.
- **Deep Health Check (`/healthz`)**: Verifies database connection, cache connectivity, and disk space.
- *Caution for TPMs*: Deep health checks can cause cascading failures. If a shared database slows down, all app servers fail health checks simultaneously, causing the load balancer to pull the entire fleet out of service. Use shallow health checks for load balancing routing and deep checks for synthetic monitoring alerts.

---

## 7. TPM Review Checklist

When scoping and reviewing ingress architecture programs:

- [ ] Is Layer 4 or Layer 7 load balancing selected based on throughput vs routing needs?
- [ ] Are active and passive health checks configured with sensible timeouts and failure thresholds?
- [ ] Is the API Gateway protected against distributed denial of service (DDoS) via rate limiting?
- [ ] Is SSL termination centralized to save backend compute cycles?
- [ ] Are correlation IDs generated at the gateway and forwarded through all downstream hops?
- [ ] Does the gateway support graceful connection-drained canary deployments (traffic splitting by percentage or header)?

---

## 8. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **Google Maglev Paper**: *Maglev: A Fast and Reliable Software Network Load Balancer* by Eisenbud et al. (USENIX NSDI, 2016).
- **Envoy Proxy Architecture**: Official Envoy Documentation (https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/arch_overview).
- **HAProxy Configuration Guide**: *HAProxy Architecture and Load Balancing Fundamentals* (HAProxy Technologies).
- *Building Microservices: Designing Fine-Grained Systems* (2nd Edition) by Sam Newman (O'Reilly Media, 2021) - Chapter 5: Integration.

SECTION 06: MODULE 1 CHAPTER 3: CACHING STRATEGIES & MEMORY TIERS
FILE: 01-foundations/03-caching-strategies.md

# Module 1.3: Distributed Caching Strategies

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 1: Foundations](./README.md) > **Chapter 1.3: Caching Strategies**

---

Caching is one of the most effective techniques to reduce latency, protect downstream databases from traffic spikes, and optimize cloud infrastructure costs. For technical program managers, understanding cache design patterns, invalidation strategies, and failure modes prevents costly production outages.

---

## 1. Multi-Tier Caching Architecture

Caching operates across every layer of the modern technology stack. A well-architected system leverages multiple cache boundaries to maximize hit rates and minimize database IOPS.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Client[Client Device / Browser] -->|1. Browser Cache: Local Storage / Service Worker| Client
    Client -->|2. Edge Cache| CDN[Content Delivery Network: Static & Geo Assets]
    CDN -->|3. Gateway Cache| GW[API Gateway / Reverse Proxy Cache: Shared HTTP Responses]
    GW -->|4. App Process Memory| App[Application Pod: In-Memory L1 Cache Caffeine/Go-Cache]
    App -->|5. Distributed Cache| DistCache[(Distributed L2 Cache: Redis / Memcached Cluster)]
    DistCache -->|6. Storage Engine Cache| DB[(Primary Database: Buffer Pool / Page Cache)]

    classDef cacheStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class CDN,GW,DistCache cacheStyle;
```

---

## 2. Read and Write Caching Patterns

The choice of caching pattern defines the consistency contract between the application, the cache, and the underlying database.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph ReadPatterns [Read Caching Strategies]
        direction LR
        CA[Cache-Aside / Lazy Loading: App coordinates cache and DB]
        RT[Read-Through: App queries Cache, Cache loads DB on miss]
    end

    subgraph WritePatterns [Write Caching Strategies]
        direction LR
        WT[Write-Through: App writes Cache, Cache writes DB synchronously]
        WB[Write-Behind / Write-Back: App writes Cache, Cache queues DB async]
        WA[Write-Around: App writes DB directly, Cache populated on read]
    end

    classDef rstyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef wstyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:1px;
    class CA,RT rstyle;
    class WT,WB,WA wstyle;
```

### 1. Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)

The application code directly coordinates between the cache and the database.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as Application Service
    participant Cache as Redis Cache
    participant DB as Database

    App->>Cache: 1. GET key
    alt Cache Hit
        Cache-->>App: 2. Return cached value (Sub-millisecond)
    else Cache Miss
        Cache-->>App: 2. Return null (miss)
        App->>DB: 3. Query primary database
        DB-->>App: 4. Return row data
        App->>Cache: 5. SET key = data (with TTL)
        App-->>App: 6. Process request
    end
```

- **Pros**: Only requested data is cached (memory efficient); cache failure does not crash the system (gracefully degrades to direct database queries).
- **Cons**: High latency penalty on cache miss (3 network round-trips); potential stale data if records are updated in the database directly without cache invalidation.

### 2. Write-Through vs Write-Behind (Write-Back)

| Dimension | Write-Through | Write-Behind (Write-Back) | Write-Around |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Data Flow** | App writes to Cache; Cache writes to DB synchronously before returning success | App writes to Cache; Cache writes to DB asynchronously in batches | App writes directly to DB; Cache is bypassed and populated on next read |
| **Write Latency** | Higher (waits for both memory cache and disk DB write to commit) | Ultra-low (returns immediately after memory write confirms) | Standard database disk write latency |
| **Consistency** | High consistency between cache and primary store | Eventual consistency; data loss risk if cache crashes before flush | Cache holds stale data unless explicitly invalidated on write |
| **Ideal For** | Financial balances, user permissions, security tokens | Heavy write workloads, clickstream tracking, IoT telemetry | Infrequently read logs, large batch file uploads |

---

## 3. Cache Eviction Policies

When memory reaches capacity limits, the cache engine must evict items to make room for new entries.

- **LRU (Least Recently Used)**: Evicts items that have not been accessed for the longest time. Standard default for general-purpose workloads.
- **LFU (Least Frequently Used)**: Tracks access counts and evicts items with the lowest access frequency. Ideal for stable, predictable hot-keys.
- **FIFO (First In, First Out)**: Evicts the oldest created items regardless of recent usage.
- **TTL (Time-to-Live)**: Automatically marks keys as expired after a configured duration (e.g. 300 seconds).

---

## 4. Redis vs Memcached

Program managers frequently navigate vendor and technology selections between Redis and Memcached.

| Feature | Redis | Memcached |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Data Structures** | Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets, Bitmaps, HyperLogLogs, Geospatial | Pure Key-Value (Strings and byte arrays only) |
| **Threading Model** | Single-threaded core engine (with multithreaded I/O since v6) | Pure Multi-threaded architecture (scales linearly across CPU cores) |
| **Persistence** | RDB snapshots, AOF (Append-Only File) logging | In-memory only (no native disk persistence) |
| **Replication & HA** | Redis Sentinel, Redis Cluster (automatic sharding and failover) | No native clustering; requires client-side consistent hashing |
| **Advanced Features** | Pub/Sub, Lua scripting, Transactions, Redis Streams | Simple, lightweight get/set memory cache |
| **Best Used For** | Rich data caching, leaderboards, rate limiters, session stores | Simple high-throughput memory caching across many CPU cores |

---

## 5. Critical Cache Failure Modes and Mitigations

These three failure modes are staple topics in architecture reviews and system design interviews.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Failures [Cache Anti-Patterns & Failures]
        direction TB
        F1[Cache Stampede / Thundering Herd]
        F2[Cache Avalanche]
        F3[Cache Penetration]
    end

    subgraph Mitigations [Engineering Mitigations]
        direction TB
        M1[Distributed Mutex Lock / Probabilistic Early Recomputation XFetch]
        M2[Jittered TTLs / Random Offset e.g. Base TTL + rand 0 to 60s]
        M3[Bloom Filters at Gateway + Cache Null Values with short TTL]
    end

    F1 ==> M1
    F2 ==> M2
    F3 ==> M3

    classDef fstyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef mstyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:1px;
    class F1,F2,F3 fstyle;
    class M1,M2,M3 mstyle;
```

### 1. Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd)
- **Problem**: A high-traffic key (e.g. homepage banner) expires. Thousands of concurrent requests experience a cache miss simultaneously and hammer the database with identical queries.
- **Mitigation**:
  - *Distributed Mutex*: Only the first thread that misses the cache acquires a lock to query the DB and update the cache; other threads wait or return previous stale data.
  - *Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch)*: Recomputes the cache value in the background before the key actually expires based on request probability.

### 2. Cache Avalanche
- **Problem**: Hundreds of thousands of keys are configured with the exact same TTL (e.g. 1 hour) during a bulk sync. All keys expire at the same second, causing the entire traffic volume to fall back on the database.
- **Mitigation**: Add random jitter to key expirations (e.g. `TTL = 3600 + random(0, 300)` seconds).

### 3. Cache Penetration
- **Problem**: Clients query non-existent keys (e.g. malicious requests for `user_id = -9999`). The cache misses, queries the database, finds nothing, and does not store a result. Every subsequent request hits the database.
- **Mitigation**:
  - *Cache Null Objects*: Store a null value with a short TTL (e.g. 60 seconds).
  - *Bloom Filters*: Position an in-memory Bloom filter in front of the cache. If the filter indicates the item definitely does not exist, return 404 immediately without touching cache or database.

---

## 6. Back-of-the-Envelope Cache Sizing (The Correct 80/20 Working Set Formula)

In system design reviews, TPMs must estimate memory requirements using distinct items rather than raw request counts:

1. **The Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule)**: 20% of the **distinct active catalog items** generate 80% of read traffic. You only need to size the fast cache tier for that hot 20%.
2. **Formula**:
   $$\text{Working Set Memory} = (\text{Total Unique Active Items} \times 0.20) \times (\text{Average Record Size} + \text{Key Overhead})$$
3. **Accounting for Redis Memory Overhead**:
   - Each key in Redis incurs approximately 60 to 100 bytes of structural overhead (`dictEntry`, `robj` header, jemalloc allocation alignment).
   - *Example*: Sizing a cache for 10 Million unique active user profiles (average profile size = 1 KB):
     $$\text{Hot Working Set} = 10,000,000 \times 0.20 = 2,000,000\text{ profiles}$$
     $$\text{Raw Data} = 2,000,000 \times 1,000\text{ bytes} = 2\text{ GB}$$
     $$\text{Key Overhead} = 2,000,000 \times 80\text{ bytes} = 160\text{ MB}$$
     $$\text{Memory with 30% Headroom Buffer} = (2\text{ GB} + 0.16\text{ GB}) \times 1.30 \approx 2.8\text{ GB RAM}$$

---

## 7. TPM Review Checklist

When validating caching designs in your program:

- [ ] Is there an explicit invalidation strategy for mutable data (TTL vs event-driven invalidation via CDC)?
- [ ] Are all cache keys set with a Time-To-Live (TTL) to prevent unbounded memory leaks?
- [ ] Are TTLs randomized with jitter to eliminate cache avalanche risks?
- [ ] What happens to application SLAs when the cache cluster restarts or fails?
- [ ] Is cache hit ratio (CHR) tracked as a critical service-level indicator (SLI)? Target CHR: 95%+ for read-heavy tiers.
- [ ] Has memory overhead for allocator fragmentation and hash table buckets been included in cluster capacity sizing?

---

## 8. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **Scaling Memcache at Facebook**: *Scaling Memcache at Facebook* by Rajesh Nishtala et al. (USENIX NSDI, 2013).
- **Redis In-Depth**: *Redis: The Definitive Guide* and Redis Official Memory Optimization Documentation (https://redis.io/docs/management/optimization/memory-optimization/).
- **Probabilistic Cache Regeneration**: *Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention* by Vattani, Chierichetti, and Lowenstein (VLDB, 2015).
- *Database Internals: A Deep Dive into How Distributed Data Systems Work* by Alex Petrov (O'Reilly Media, 2019) - Chapter 12: Distributed Caching.

Data architecture dictates the durability, scalability, and transactional integrity of any distributed platform. # Module 2.1: Databases: Relational vs NoSQL vs NewSQL

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 2: Data Architecture](./README.md) > **Chapter 2.1: Databases SQL vs NoSQL vs NewSQL**

---

Data architecture is the foundation of any software system. Choosing the right database technology affects developer velocity, schema migration complexity, query performance, and long-term operating costs. Technical program managers must navigate trade-offs between structured consistency and horizontal elasticity.

---

## 1. ACID vs BASE Philosophy

Database systems operate under two distinct philosophical frameworks governing transactions and consistency.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ACID [ACID Framework: Relational Systems]
        A[Atomicity: All operations succeed or none do]
        C[Consistency: Data satisfies all schema constraints]
        I[Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not cross-contaminate]
        D[Durability: Committed data survives crashes and power loss]
    end

    subgraph BASE [BASE Framework: Distributed NoSQL Systems]
        BA[Basically Available: System guarantees availability]
        S[Soft State: System state may drift without active input]
        E[Eventual Consistency: Replicas converge given time]
    end

    classDef acidStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef baseStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class A,C,I,D acidStyle;
    class BA,S,E baseStyle;
```

---

## 2. The Database Landscape

Modern architectures employ specialized databases tailored to specific access patterns rather than forcing a single engine to solve all problems.

```mermaid
graph TD
    Root[Database Categories] --> Relational[Relational / RDBMS]
    Root --> NoSQL[NoSQL Family]
    Root --> NewSQL[NewSQL Distributed SQL]

    Relational --> R1[PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle]
    
    NoSQL --> KV[Key-Value: Redis, AWS DynamoDB]
    NoSQL --> Doc[Document: MongoDB, Couchbase]
    NoSQL --> Col[Wide-Column: Apache Cassandra, ScyllaDB]
    NoSQL --> Graph[Graph: Neo4j, Amazon Neptune]
    NoSQL --> TS[Time-Series: InfluxDB, TimescaleDB]

    NewSQL --> NS1[Google Cloud Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB]

    classDef catStyle fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#334155,stroke-width:1px;
    class Root,Relational,NoSQL,NewSQL catStyle;
```

### Comprehensive Database Comparison

| Database Type | Primary Data Model | Strengths | Weaknesses | Best Use Cases |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Relational (RDBMS)** | Tables, Rows, Foreign Keys | Strict ACID transactions, complex SQL joins, mature tooling | Difficult to shard horizontally; rigid schema migrations | Financial ledgers, ERP, CRM, core user accounts |
| **Key-Value** | Opaque Key mapped to Value | Single-digit millisecond latency, massive scale, simple API | No rich querying on values; limited aggregation | Session stores, user shopping carts, cache lookup |
| **Document** | Hierarchical JSON / BSON documents | Flexible schema, rapid prototyping, nested document queries | Memory hungry, potential document duplication | Content management systems, product catalogs, user profiles |
| **Wide-Column** | Keyspace, Column Families, Sparse Rows | Linear write scalability across hundreds of nodes, high availability | No ACID transactions across partitions; no joins | IoT telemetry, clickstream logging, messaging history |
| **Graph** | Nodes, Edges, Properties | Ultra-fast traversal of deep relationships ($O(1)$ pointer hops) | Difficult to partition across clusters; niche query languages | Social networks, fraud detection graphs, recommendation engines |
| **NewSQL** | Relational SQL with Distributed Consensus | Global ACID transactions, horizontal scale, automated sharding | High operational complexity, higher write latency (consensus overhead) | Global multi-region banking, large-scale order checkout |

---

## 3. Storage Engine Internals: B-Trees vs LSM-Trees

Understanding how databases write data to disk explains why certain engines excel at reads while others excel at writes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph BTree [B-Tree Engine: Read-Optimized e.g. PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB]
        BT1[In-place disk page updates] --> BT2[Pages organized in balanced multi-way tree]
        BT2 --> BT3[Fast point lookups: O log N disk seeks]
        BT3 --> BT4[Slower random writes: Requires writing full 8KB/16KB disk pages]
    end

    subgraph LSMTree [LSM-Tree Engine: Write-Optimized e.g. Cassandra, RocksDB]
        LSM1[Incoming Write -> Fast In-Memory MemTable] --> LSM2[Append to Write-Ahead Log WAL on disk]
        LSM2 --> LSM3[MemTable flushes sequentially to SSTables on disk]
        LSM3 --> LSM4[Background Compaction merges SSTables]
        LSM4 --> LSM5[Slower reads: Check MemTable, Bloom filters, multiple SSTables]
    end

    classDef btStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef lsmStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class BTree btStyle;
    class LSMTree lsmStyle;
```

### Core Takeaway for TPMs
- Use **B-Tree engines** (PostgreSQL, MySQL) when your application has high read ratios (e.g. 90% reads, 10% writes) and requires predictable query performance.
- Use **LSM-Tree engines** (Cassandra, RocksDB, ScyllaDB) when your application handles high-velocity write streams (e.g. 100,000 writes/sec of IoT sensors or log ingestion) because all disk writes are sequential.

---

## 4. Indexing Fundamentals and Trade-offs

Indexes are separate data structures created to accelerate read queries. However, they introduce hidden operational costs.

### Index Mechanics
- **Clustered / Primary Index**: Determines the physical ordering of data on disk (usually the Primary Key). Each table can have only one clustered index.
- **Non-Clustered / Secondary Index**: A separate tree structure containing the indexed column value and a pointer back to the primary row.
- **Composite Index**: An index spanning multiple columns (e.g. `(tenant_id, created_at)`). Follows the Leftmost Prefix Rule; queries must filter by `tenant_id` to utilize the index.

### The Index Penalty
Every write (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) must synchronously update all defined secondary indexes on the table.
- A table with 10 secondary indexes experiences up to 10x write amplification.
- Program managers should audit indexes before major feature launches to drop unused indexes and preserve write throughput.

---

## 5. Polyglot Persistence: The Modern Standard

Enterprise applications rarely rely on a single database. Instead, they implement polyglot persistence: routing specific domains to purpose-built data stores.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client[Web & Mobile Clients] --> Gateway[API Gateway]
    
    Gateway --> SvcUser[User Service]
    Gateway --> SvcOrder[Order Service]
    Gateway --> SvcSearch[Catalog Search]
    Gateway --> SvcFeed[Activity Feed]

    SvcUser --> DB_User[(PostgreSQL: User Accounts & Roles)]
    SvcOrder --> DB_Order[(Spanner / CockroachDB: ACID Transactions)]
    SvcSearch --> DB_Search[(Elasticsearch: Full-Text Product Search)]
    SvcFeed --> DB_Feed[(Cassandra: High-Throughput Timeline Feed)]

    classDef dbsStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:1px;
    class DB_User,DB_Order,DB_Search,DB_Feed dbsStyle;
```

---

## 6. TPM Review Checklist

When reviewing data store proposals:

- [ ] Does the business domain require strict ACID transactional guarantees (e.g. financial ledgers)?
- [ ] What is the read-to-write ratio (e.g. 10:1 vs 1:5)?
- [ ] Is the data structure relational with frequent joins, or hierarchical document data?
- [ ] How will schema migrations be managed without locking tables or degrading production latency?
- [ ] Are secondary indexes audited and restricted to high-frequency query paths?
- [ ] Has the team defined retention and archival policies for older records (e.g. cold storage partitioning)?

---

## 7. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **Google Spanner Paper**: *Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database* by James C. Corbett et al. (OSDI, 2012).
- **Amazon Dynamo Paper**: *Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store* by Giuseppe DeCandia et al. (SOSP, 2007).
- **Relational Model Foundation**: *A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks* by E. F. Codd (Communications of the ACM, 1970).
- *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly Media, 2017) - Chapter 3: Storage and Retrieval.

SECTION 09: MODULE 2 CHAPTER 2: SHARDING, REPLICATION & PARTITIONING
