# Module 2.2: Database Replication, Sharding, and Consistent Hashing

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 2: Data Architecture](./README.md) > **Chapter 2.2: Replication, Sharding & Consistent Hashing**

---

When data volumes exceed the capacity of a single physical server, or read traffic threatens to overwhelm a single database instance, systems must scale horizontally. Technical program managers must understand how replication provides fault tolerance and read scale, while sharding partitions write workloads.

---

## 1. Database Replication Topologies

Replication creates redundant copies of data across multiple physical machines to ensure high availability and survivability during hardware failures.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph SingleLeader [Single-Leader / Master-Replica]
        App1[Application Tier] -->|Synchronous Writes| Leader[Primary / Leader Node]
        Leader -->|Asynchronous Replication Stream| Replica1[Read Replica 1]
        Leader -->|Asynchronous Replication Stream| Replica2[Read Replica 2]
        App1 -->|Read Queries| Replica1
        App1 -->|Read Queries| Replica2
    end

    subgraph Leaderless [Leaderless / Quorum Replication]
        App2[Application / Coordinator] -->|Write to Quorum W=2| NodeA[Node A]
        App2 -->|Write to Quorum W=2| NodeB[Node B]
        App2 -.->|Write Drops / Network Split| NodeC[Node C]
    end

    classDef sStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef lStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:1px;
    class SingleLeader sStyle;
    class Leaderless lStyle;
```

### Replication Topology Comparison

| Model | Write Mechanism | Read Mechanism | Strengths | Operational Risks | Example Systems |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Single-Leader** | Single master node accepts all writes | Master or read replicas accept read queries | Simple write ordering; no write conflict resolution required | Master node is single point of failure; replication lag causes stale reads | MySQL, PostgreSQL, Redis |
| **Multi-Leader** | Multiple master nodes in different data centers accept writes | Local master or local replicas serve reads | Low write latency across continents; survives DC outages | Complex write conflicts require resolution (LWW or CRDTs) | Multi-region Couchbase, DynamoDB Global Tables |
| **Leaderless** | Writes sent to multiple peers simultaneously | Reads query multiple peers; resolves versions via quorum | Highly available; no failover pauses; tolerates node drops | Inconsistent reads if quorum formula not met; repair overhead | Apache Cassandra, AWS DynamoDB, ScyllaDB |

---

## 2. Replication Lag and Consistency Guarantees

In asynchronous replication, replicas inevitably lag behind the primary node. This delay causes common user-visible bugs:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant User as End User
    participant App as App Server
    participant Primary as Primary DB
    participant Replica as Read Replica

    User->>App: 1. POST /comment ("Great post!")
    App->>Primary: 2. INSERT comment
    Primary-->>App: 3. Success (Committed)
    App-->>User: 4. 201 Created
    
    Note over Primary,Replica: Network delay / replication lag (500ms)
    
    User->>App: 5. GET /comments (Refresh page immediately)
    App->>Replica: 6. SELECT comments
    Replica-->>App: 7. Comment not found (Stale data!)
    App-->>User: 8. Renders page without user comment!
```

### Critical Consistency Patterns for TPMs
1. **Read-Your-Own-Writes Consistency**: Guarantees that if a user updates data, their subsequent reads reflect that update.
   - *Implementation*: Route reads for the updating user to the primary database for 10 seconds post-write, while routing other users to read replicas.
2. **Monotonic Reads**: Guarantees that a user will never see time move backward (e.g. reading from an up-to-date replica on request 1, then hitting a lagging replica on request 2).
   - *Implementation*: Hash the user ID to consistently route a given user to the same replica instance.

---

## 3. Data Partitioning / Sharding Strategies

When dataset size exceeds the disk limit of a single machine or write throughput saturates CPU cores, the database must be partitioned (sharded).

```mermaid
graph TD
    Sharding[Database Sharding Strategies] --> Range[Range-Based Sharding]
    Sharding --> Hash[Hash-Based Sharding]
    Sharding --> Directory[Directory / Lookup Sharding]

    Range --> R1[Shard 1: A-H, Shard 2: I-P, Shard 3: Q-Z]
    Hash --> H1[Shard = hash key modulo N]
    Directory --> D1[Central Lookup Service maps Entity ID to Shard ID]

    classDef stratStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class Range,Hash,Directory stratStyle;
```

### Sharding Trade-off Matrix

| Strategy | Logic | Pros | Cons |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Range-Based** | Partitions by value ranges (e.g. dates: 2024-Q1, 2024-Q2) | Efficient range queries (e.g. all transactions in March) | Hot spots occur when high write volumes target the current timestamp |
| **Hash-Based** | Partitions using hash function: `hash(user_id) % N` | Uniform write distribution; eliminates date hot spots | Range queries require querying every single shard (Scatter-Gather) |
| **Directory-Based** | Lookup service maintains mapping table of key to shard | Maximum flexibility; shards can be moved dynamically | Directory lookup service becomes a single point of failure and bottleneck |

---

## 4. Consistent Hashing

Traditional modulo hashing (`hash(key) % N`) breaks down when nodes are added or removed: almost 100% of keys must be reshuffled, causing massive cache misses and database thrashing. Consistent hashing solves this problem.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph HashRing [Consistent Hashing Ring: 0 to 2^32 - 1]
        direction TB
        NodeA[Node A Virtual Nodes: A1, A2, A3]
        NodeB[Node B Virtual Nodes: B1, B2, B3]
        NodeC[Node C Virtual Nodes: C1, C2, C3]
    end

    Key1[Key 1] -->|Hashes to Ring -> Moves Clockwise| NodeA
    Key2[Key 2] -->|Hashes to Ring -> Moves Clockwise| NodeB
    Key3[Key 3] -->|Hashes to Ring -> Moves Clockwise| NodeC

    classDef ringStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class HashRing ringStyle;
```

### Key Principles of Consistent Hashing

1. **Circular Hash Ring**: The output of the hash function is mapped to a circular range (from 0 to $2^{32} - 1$).
2. **Clockwise Assignment**: Both servers and data keys are hashed onto the ring. A key is assigned to the first server encountered moving clockwise.
3. **Minimal Key Rebalancing**: When a new server is added, only $K/N$ keys need to be reassigned (where $K$ is total keys, and $N$ is number of servers).
4. **Virtual Nodes (vnodes)**: To prevent uneven data distribution, each physical machine is assigned multiple virtual nodes (e.g. 100 to 256 points on the ring). This ensures uniform distribution and prevents hot spots.

---

## 5. Sharding Risks and the TPM Mitigation Matrix

Sharding introduces substantial architectural complexity. Technical program managers should ensure teams have evaluated the following risks:

| Sharding Risk | Description | Engineering Mitigation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **The Celebrity Problem (Hot Shard)** | A single high-volume entity (e.g. a celebrity with 50M followers) overloads a single shard | Append random salt to partition keys (e.g. `celebrity_id + "_" + rand(0, 10)`); scatter reads and aggregate |
| **Cross-Shard Joins** | SQL queries requiring joins across data sitting on different physical shards cause extreme latency | Denormalize data, duplicate reference tables across all shards, or execute joins at the application layer |
| **Distributed Transactions** | Updating records across multiple shards requires Two-Phase Commit (2PC), which kills throughput | Colocate related entities on the same shard using composite shard keys (e.g. `tenant_id:order_id`) |
| **Re-sharding Operations** | Splitting an existing shard into two under live production traffic | Dual-writing to old and new shards, running background backfill, validating data consistency, and cutting over |

---

## 6. TPM Review Checklist

Before signing off on database scaling architectures:

- [ ] Has the team confirmed that vertical scaling, indexing optimization, and caching are exhausted before committing to sharding?
- [ ] Is the partition key chosen with high cardinality to prevent uneven data skews?
- [ ] What is the planned re-sharding trigger (e.g. when any shard exceeds 70% storage capacity)?
- [ ] Does the application support Read-Your-Own-Writes consistency for critical user paths?
- [ ] Is cross-datacenter replication monitoring configured with alert thresholds for replication lag (e.g. alert if lag > 1000ms)?

---

## 7. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **Consistent Hashing Foundation**: *Consistent Hashing and Random Trees: Distributed Caching Protocols for Relieving Hot Spots on the World Wide Web* by David Karger et al. (ACM STOC, 1997).
- *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly Media, 2017) - Chapter 5: Replication & Chapter 6: Partitioning.
- **Amazon Dynamo Paper**: *Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store* by Giuseppe DeCandia et al. (SOSP, 2007) - Sections on Quorum and Consistent Hashing.
- *Database Internals* by Alex Petrov (O'Reilly Media, 2019) - Part II: Distributed Systems.


================================================================================
SECTION 10: MODULE 2 CHAPTER 3: CAP AND PACELC THEOREMS IN PRACTICE
FILE: 02-data-architecture/03-cap-pacelc-theorems.md
================================================================================

# Module 2.3: The CAP and PACELC Theorems

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 2: Data Architecture](./README.md) > **Chapter 2.3: The CAP and PACELC Theorems**

---

Distributed systems must navigate fundamental trade-offs imposed by the laws of physics and network unreliability. The CAP and PACELC theorems provide the theoretical foundation for explaining why no distributed database can offer both instantaneous global consistency and uninterrupted availability during network splits.

---

## 1. The CAP Theorem Explained

Formulated by Eric Brewer and later proved by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch, the CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two out of three properties simultaneously:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph CAP [The CAP Theorem Core Dimensions]
        C[Consistency: Every read receives the most recent write or an error]
        A[Availability: Every non-failing node returns a non-error response]
        P[Partition Tolerance: System operates despite arbitrary packet drops]
    end

    classDef capStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class C,A,P capStyle;
```

### The Fundamental Reality: Partition Tolerance is Non-Negotiable
In physical networks, routers fail, optical fiber cables get cut, and network switches drop packets. Therefore, a distributed system **must** tolerate partitions ($P$). The real architectural choice is:

> **In the presence of a network partition ($P$), does the system choose Consistency ($CP$) or Availability ($AP$)?**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    PartitionEvent{Network Partition Occurs!} --> PathCP[Choose CP: Reject Writes / Pause Service]
    PartitionEvent --> PathAP[Choose AP: Accept Writes on Both Sides]

    PathCP --> ResCP[Guarantees no stale or conflicting data, but clients experience errors]
    PathAP --> ResAP[Nodes continue serving requests locally, trading cross-partition consistency]

    classDef cpStyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef apStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class PathCP,ResCP cpStyle;
    class PathAP,ResAP apStyle;
```

---

## 2. CP Systems vs AP Systems

| System Type | Core Behavior during Network Split | Representative Databases | Typical Business Domains |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance)** | Unreachable nodes reject requests or time out until the partition heals to prevent data divergence | Google Cloud Spanner, CockroachDB, HBase, Redis Sentinel, ZooKeeper | Financial balances, stock inventory, flight seat booking, identity tokens |
| **AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance)** | Nodes on each side of the split accept reads and writes. Data reconciles when partition heals | Apache Cassandra, AWS DynamoDB (default), Couchbase, ScyllaDB | Social feeds, video view counts, shopping cart items, telemetry logs |

---

## 3. The PACELC Theorem: Beyond Failure States

The CAP theorem only describes what happens when the system fails (during a network partition). But distributed systems spend 99.9% of their operating time in a healthy, unpartitioned state.

Daniel Abadi developed the **PACELC theorem** to address normal state trade-offs:

$$\text{If } \mathbf{P} \text{ (Partition): Choose } \mathbf{A} \text{ or } \mathbf{C}; \quad \text{EL} \text{se: Choose } \mathbf{L} \text{ (Latency) or } \mathbf{C} \text{ (Consistency)}$$

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start[System State] --> IsPart{Is there an active network partition?}
    
    IsPart -->|Yes: Partition P| ChoiceP{Trade-off:}
    ChoiceP -->|A| AP[Availability: Cassandra, DynamoDB]
    ChoiceP -->|C| CP[Consistency: Spanner, HBase]

    IsPart -->|No: Else E| ChoiceE{Trade-off:}
    ChoiceE -->|L| EL[Low Latency: Replicate async, return immediately]
    ChoiceE -->|C| EC[High Consistency: Wait for multi-node consensus round-trips]

    classDef boxStyle fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#334155,stroke-width:1px;
    class Start,IsPart,ChoiceP,ChoiceE boxStyle;
```

### PACELC Database Classification

| Database | PACELC Classification | Architectural Mechanics |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **DynamoDB** | **PA / EL** | If partitioned: Availability over Consistency. Else: Low Latency over strong consistency (asynchronous replication by default). |
| **Cassandra** | **PA / EL** | Tunable consistency, but defaults to high availability and low latency with eventual consistency. |
| **Cloud Spanner** | **PC / EC** | TrueTime atomic clocks enforce strict serializability. Consistency is prioritized during partitions and normal operations. |
| **MongoDB** | **PC / EC** | Routes primary writes with replica acknowledgement. Defaults to consistency over availability and latency. |
| **PostgreSQL (Async Replica)** | **PC / EL** | Single master enforces consistency on writes. Replicas accept lag for low-latency read queries. |

---

## 4. The Consistency Spectrum

Consistency in distributed systems is not binary (strong vs eventual). It exists on a continuum:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S1[Strict / Linearizable Consistency] --> S2[Sequential Consistency]
    S2 --> S3[Causal Consistency]
    S3 --> S4[Read-Your-Own-Writes]
    S4 --> S5[Eventual Consistency]

    classDef specStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:1px;
    class S1,S2,S3,S4,S5 specStyle;
```

1. **Linearizability (Strongest)**: Every read sees the latest globally committed write instantaneously, as if there were only one copy of data in the universe. Highest latency penalty.
2. **Sequential Consistency**: Operations appear in the order defined by the program, and all nodes see the same sequence of operations.
3. **Causal Consistency**: Causally related events (e.g. Question $\rightarrow$ Answer) appear in order across all nodes; unrelated operations can be observed in different orders.
4. **Eventual Consistency (Weakest)**: If no new writes occur, all replicas eventually converge to the same value. Lowest latency and highest throughput.

---

## 5. TPM Decision Framework: Aligning Business with Architecture

As a program manager, you must translate business requirements into distributed consistency parameters:

| Business Domain | Required Behavior | Recommended Choice | Rationale |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Banking Ledger** | Prevent negative balance and double-spending | **CP / EC** | Financial balance errors destroy trust and violate statutory regulatory compliance. |
| **E-Commerce Product Reviews** | Show newly posted reviews to shoppers | **AP / EL** | A shopper seeing a review 2 seconds late has zero business impact. Availability and low page latency drive sales. |
| **Collaborative Document Editing** | Avoid losing keystrokes during connection drops | **AP with CRDTs** | Local updates render with zero latency; Conflict-free Replicated Data Types merge edits deterministically. |
| **Inventory Reservation** | Ensure item is not sold to two buyers | **CP / EC** | Overselling generates customer support escalations, cancellation penalties, and logistical overhead. |

---

## 6. TPM Review Checklist

When evaluating distributed storage trade-offs:

- [ ] Does the product experience tolerate eventual consistency (stale reads of 50ms to 2000ms)?
- [ ] For AP systems, how are write conflicts resolved (Last-Write-Wins, vector clocks, or application-level merges)?
- [ ] What is the exact customer experience when a network partition forces a CP system to reject requests?
- [ ] Has the engineering team configured timeout thresholds and circuit breakers for quorum reads?
- [ ] Are business metrics (conversion rates, revenue) balanced against the latency penalty of strong consistency?

---

## 7. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **CAP Proof**: *Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services* by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch (ACM SIGACT News, 2002).
- **CAP 12-Year Retrospective**: *CAP Twelve Years Later: How the Rules Have Changed* by Eric Brewer (IEEE Computer, 2012).
- **PACELC Formulation**: *Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design: CAP is Only Part of the Story* by Daniel J. Abadi (IEEE Computer, 2012).
- *Principles of Eventual Consistency* by Sebastian Burckhardt (Foundations and Trends in Programming Languages, 2014).

SECTION 11: MODULE 2 CHAPTER 4: MESSAGE QUEUES & EVENT STREAMING
FILE: 02-data-architecture/04-message-queues-streaming.md
================================================================================

# Module 2.4: Asynchronous Messaging and Event Streaming

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 2: Data Architecture](./README.md) > **Chapter 2.4: Messaging & Event Streaming**

---

Synchronous HTTP calls couple distributed microservices in time and availability: if Service B is slow or down, Service A fails as well. Asynchronous messaging decouples systems, absorbs traffic bursts, and enables event-driven architectures. Technical program managers must distinguish between traditional message queues and distributed event streaming platforms.

---

## 1. Why Asynchronous Messaging Matters

Asynchronous communication provides three foundational benefits for large-scale architectures:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Benefits [Asynchronous Architecture Benefits]
        B1[Temporal Decoupling: Producer does not wait for Consumer]
        B2[Traffic Leveling: Buffer absorbs bursty peak spikes]
        B3[Failure Isolation: Consumer outage does not break producer API]
    end

    classDef bStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class B1,B2,B3 bStyle;
```

---

## 2. Message Queues vs Distributed Event Streams

While both technologies pass data asynchronously, their architectural models and consumption semantics are fundamentally different.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph TraditionalQueue [Traditional Message Queue: RabbitMQ, AWS SQS]
        direction TB
        P1[Producer] --> Q[Queue: FIFO Buffer]
        Q --> C1[Consumer A: Pulls Message 1]
        Q --> C2[Consumer B: Pulls Message 2]
        Note over Q: Message is deleted immediately once acknowledged
    end

    subgraph EventStream [Distributed Event Stream: Apache Kafka, AWS Kinesis]
        direction TB
        P2[Producer] --> Log[(Append-Only Commit Log / Partitions)]
        Log --> CG1[Consumer Group 1: Analytics Offset = 4]
        Log --> CG2[Consumer Group 2: Notifications Offset = 8]
        Note over Log: Messages are retained for days/weeks. Multiple groups read independently.
    end

    classDef tqStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef esStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class TraditionalQueue tqStyle;
    class EventStream esStyle;
```

### Direct Technology Comparison

| Dimension | Message Queues (RabbitMQ, SQS) | Event Streams (Kafka, Kinesis) | Architectural Decision Criteria |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Data Retention** | Ephemeral: Messages deleted upon consumer acknowledgement | Persistent: Retained on disk by duration (e.g. 7 days) or size limit | Choose Kafka if events need replaying for analytics or auditing |
| **Message Ordering** | Strict per-queue (or best-effort in standard SQS) | Strict total order within a single partition | Choose Kafka for strict per-entity chronological ordering |
| **Consumption Model** | Point-to-point work distribution: one consumer consumes each message | Publish-Subscribe log: multiple independent consumer groups read at own pace | Choose SQS for simple task workers; Kafka for multiple domain subscribers |
| **Replayability** | Cannot rewind and replay past messages | Consumers can reset offsets and replay historic events | Kafka enables backfilling new microservices with past events |
| **Peak Throughput** | Thousands of messages per second | Millions of events per second via sequential disk I/O and batching | Kafka for extreme high-volume telemetry and clickstreams |
| **Best Used For** | Asynchronous task execution, long-running batch jobs, simple workflows | Real-time event streams, clickstream tracking, financial ledgers, event sourcing | Evaluate operational maintenance overhead vs scale requirements |

---

## 3. Message Delivery Semantics

Understanding delivery guarantees is critical when designing payment processing, order fulfillment, and user notifications.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A1[At-Most-Once] -->|Risk: Data Loss| R1[No retries. Message sent once. Best for non-critical logs.]
    A2[At-Least-Once] -->|Risk: Duplication| R2[Retries on failure. Requires Idempotent Consumers.]
    A3[Exactly-Once] -->|Highest Complexity| R3[Two-phase transactions or deduplication tokens.]

    classDef gStyle fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#334155,stroke-width:1px;
    class A1,A2,A3 gStyle;
```

### The Pragmatic Reality: At-Least-Once + Idempotency
Achieving true end-to-end "exactly-once" delivery across multiple network boundaries is computationally expensive and complex. 

The industry gold standard for high-throughput distributed systems is:

$$\text{At-Least-Once Delivery} + \text{Idempotent Consumer Processing} = \text{Effective Exactly-Once Business Outcome}$$

- **Idempotency Key**: The producer generates a unique transaction UUID (e.g. `idem_key_987213`).
- **Consumer Deduplication**: The consumer checks a fast key-value store (e.g. Redis) before processing. If the key was already processed, it acknowledges the message and returns the previous result without repeating side effects.

---

## 4. Resilience Patterns: Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) and Poison Pills

A **Poison Pill** is a malformed message (e.g. invalid JSON syntax or corrupted payload) that causes the consumer application to crash every time it attempts processing.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Q as Main Message Queue
    participant C as Consumer Worker
    participant DLQ as Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)
    participant Alert as PagerDuty / Ops Team

    Q->>C: Deliver Message #101
    Note over C: JSON Parsing Error! (Exception)
    C-->>Q: NACK (Negative Ack) / Retry
    Note over Q: Retry attempt 1, 2, 3... Max Retries Exceeded!
    Q->>DLQ: Route to Dead Letter Queue
    DLQ->>Alert: Trigger High-Priority Alert
    Note over C: Worker resumes healthy processing of Message #102
```

### Operational Rules for DLQs
1. **Never drop poison pills silently**: Always route unprocessable messages to a DLQ for offline inspection.
2. **Alerting on DLQ depth**: Any message entering a DLQ should generate an alert for engineering investigation.
3. **Replay capability**: Provide automated tooling or scripts to redrive corrected messages from the DLQ back to the main queue once the bug is resolved.

---

## 5. Kafka Core Architecture: Partitions and Consumer Groups

To achieve horizontal scalability, Apache Kafka partitions topics across multiple broker machines.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph TopicOrders [Topic: orders (3 Partitions)]
        P0[Partition 0: Events for User ID hash % 3 == 0]
        P1[Partition 1: Events for User ID hash % 3 == 1]
        P2[Partition 2: Events for User ID hash % 3 == 2]
    end

    subgraph ConsumerGroup [Consumer Group: Order Processing Fleet]
        C1[Pod 1 reads Partition 0]
        C2[Pod 2 reads Partition 1]
        C3[Pod 3 reads Partition 2]
    end

    P0 --> C1
    P1 --> C2
    P2 --> C3

    classDef partStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef podStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class P0,P1,P2 partStyle;
    class C1,C2,C3 podStyle;
```

### Partition Sizing and Scaling Rules
- **Concurrency Unit**: The number of partitions determines the maximum number of parallel consumers in a consumer group. If a topic has 3 partitions, adding a 4th consumer pod results in the 4th pod sitting idle.
- **Partition Key Selection**: Always partition by entity ID (e.g. `order_id` or `user_id`) to ensure all events for that specific entity arrive in strict chronological order at the same consumer pod.

---

## 6. TPM Review Checklist

When leading programs involving asynchronous messaging infrastructure:

- [ ] Is asynchronous communication selected for tasks that do not require instant synchronous user response?
- [ ] Are consumers engineered to be strictly idempotent to handle duplicate deliveries?
- [ ] Is a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) configured with a retry policy (e.g. max 3 retries with exponential backoff)?
- [ ] Is consumer lag tracked as a tier-1 operational metric with automated alerts?
- [ ] Has the team sized topic partitions appropriately to match projected peak consumer parallelism?
- [ ] What is the data retention policy (e.g. 7 days vs 30 days) and how does disk growth impact cloud storage budgets?

---

## 7. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **Apache Kafka Paper**: *Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing* by Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede, and Jun Rao (NetDB, 2011).
- **The Log Architecture**: *The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction* by Jay Kreps (LinkedIn Engineering Blog, 2013).
- **Enterprise Integration Patterns**: *Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions* by Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf (Addison-Wesley, 2003).
- *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly Media, 2017) - Chapter 11: Stream Processing.

# Module 3: System Resilience, Scale, and Non-Functional Requirements

[Home](../README.md) > **Module 3: Resilience & Scale**

---

## Overview

A system that functions perfectly in a development environment can quickly fail in production when subjected to unpredictable real-world traffic spikes, hardware crashes, and network latency anomalies. This module equips Technical Program Managers with the frameworks and patterns needed to design resilient, fault-tolerant, horizontally scalable architectures that meet strict contractual Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

---

## Module Learning Objectives

1. **Stateless Scalability**: Architect stateless application tiers by externalizing session state, decoupling reads and writes via CQRS, and implementing graceful auto-scaling policies.
2. **Failure Isolation**: Protect platforms from cascading failures using Circuit Breakers, Exponential Backoff with randomized full jitter, Bulkheads, and distributed Idempotency Keys.
3. **Rate Limiting**: Evaluate rate-limiting algorithms (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window Counter) to protect downstream services from abusive traffic and API scraping.
4. **Reliability Governance**: Master the SLI/SLO/SLA hierarchy, calculate high availability ("The Nines") mathematics, enforce Error Budget policies, and establish Disaster Recovery (RPO/RTO) baselines.

---

## Chapter Directory

| Chapter | Title | Focus Areas | Key Trade-offs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **[3.1](./01-scalability-patterns.md)** | Architectural Scalability Patterns | Scale-Up vs Scale-Out, stateless application tier, CQRS, background workers | Infrastructure cost vs elasticity, eventual read consistency |
| **[3.2](./02-fault-tolerance-patterns.md)** | Fault Tolerance, Resilience & Rate Limiting | Circuit breakers, exponential backoff + jitter, rate limiting, bulkheads | Failure isolation vs fallback complexity, client retry storms |
| **[3.3](./03-slas-slis-slos-nfrs.md)** | High Availability, NFRs & Disaster Recovery | SLI/SLO/SLA, "The Nines" math, error budgets, RPO/RTO, DR topologies | Availability vs infrastructure cost, feature velocity vs reliability |

---

## Suggested Prerequisites

- Completion of [Module 1: Foundations](../01-foundations/README.md) and [Module 2: Data Architecture](../02-data-architecture/README.md).
- Understanding of basic probability and statistical distributions (p50, p95, p99 latency percentiles).

SECTION 13: MODULE 3 CHAPTER 1: SCALABILITY PATTERNS & MICROSERVICES

# Module 3.1: Architectural Scalability Patterns

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 3: Resilience & Scale](./README.md) > **Chapter 3.1: Architectural Scalability Patterns**

---

Scalability describes a system's capacity to handle increased workload without compromising performance or linearly exploding operational costs. For technical program managers, scaling is not just an engineering problem; it dictates cloud budget predictability, headcount planning, and customer SLA compliance during business growth.

---

## 1. Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling

Every system design journey begins with deciding between scaling up or scaling out.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph ScaleUp [Vertical Scaling: Scale-Up]
        direction TB
        V1[Single Server: 4 CPU / 16GB RAM] -->|Upgrade Hardware| V2[Single Server: 64 CPU / 512GB RAM]
    end

    subgraph ScaleOut [Horizontal Scaling: Scale-Out]
        direction TB
        H1[Single Server: 4 CPU / 16GB] -->|Add Identical Nodes Behind LB| H2[Cluster of 20 Identical Nodes]
    end

    classDef sUpStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef sOutStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class ScaleUp sUpStyle;
    class ScaleOut sOutStyle;
```

### Comprehensive Comparison

| Metric | Vertical Scaling (Scale-Up) | Horizontal Scaling (Scale-Out) | Architectural Trade-off |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hardware Limit** | Hard ceiling: finite physical RAM and CPU sockets per motherboard | Elastic: add commodity virtual machines or container pods | Horizontal scales indefinitely; vertical hits hardware caps |
| **Downtime Impact** | Often requires machine reboot or maintenance window to resize | Rolling additions and removals without downtime | Horizontal provides high release agility |
| **Failure Domain** | Single point of failure: hardware death collapses service | High fault tolerance: loss of one node is absorbed by cluster | Horizontal eliminates single points of failure |
| **Architectural Complexity** | Zero code changes: runs identical monolithic code | Requires stateless code, distributed sessions, and routing | Vertical is faster initially; horizontal scales long-term |
| **Cost Curve** | Exponential cost curve for specialized multi-terabyte RAM boxes | Linear cost curve: pay for commodity cloud compute dynamically | Horizontal allows dynamic down-scaling during off-peak hours |

---

## 2. The Stateless Application Tier

The prerequisite for true horizontal scalability is making application servers **stateless**. If an application server stores user sessions, uploaded files, or websocket state in local memory, requests from the same user cannot be routed freely to other instances.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph StatefulAntiPattern [Stateful Anti-Pattern: Sticky Sessions Required]
        ClientA[User A] --> LBA[Load Balancer]
        LBA -->|Session in Node 1 Memory| Node1[App Server 1]
        Note over Node1: If Server 1 crashes, User A session is lost!
    end

    subgraph StatelessPattern [Stateless Best Practice: Externalized State]
        ClientB[User B] --> LBB[Load Balancer]
        LBB --> AnyNode[Any App Server Pod 1, 2, or N]
        AnyNode <--> SharedCache[(Shared Redis Cluster: Session Store)]
        AnyNode <--> SharedStore[(Shared Object Store S3: File Uploads)]
    end

    classDef badStyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef goodStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:1px;
    class StatefulAntiPattern badStyle;
    class StatelessPattern goodStyle;
```

### Eliminating State from Application Nodes
1. **User Authentication**: Use self-contained JSON Web Tokens (JWT) verified via cryptographic keys, or store session IDs in an external, highly available Redis cluster.
2. **File Storage**: Never save uploaded files to local disk paths (e.g. `/var/uploads`). Write directly to distributed object storage (AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage).
3. **Background Tasks**: Offload long-running computations from web threads to dedicated asynchronous worker pools.

---

## 3. Read vs Write Optimization: The CQRS Pattern

In most consumer applications, read traffic dwarfs write traffic by factors of 10:1 to 100:1. Coupling reads and writes to the same database model creates contention and slows down response times.

**CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)** separates read operations from mutation operations into independent models:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client[Web / Mobile Clients] --> Gateway[API Gateway]
    
    Gateway -->|Command: POST /orders| CmdSvc[Order Write Service]
    Gateway -->|Query: GET /orders| QuerySvc[Order Read Service]

    CmdSvc -->|ACID Write| WriteDB[(Primary Write DB: PostgreSQL / Spanner)]
    WriteDB -->|CDC / Kafka Event Stream| EventStream[(Event Stream)]
    EventStream -->|Materialize Views| QueryDB[(Read DB: Elasticsearch / Redis)]
    QuerySvc -->|Ultra-Fast Read| QueryDB

    classDef writeStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef readStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:1px;
    class CmdSvc,WriteDB writeStyle;
    class QuerySvc,QueryDB readStyle;
```

### CQRS Programmatic Benefits
- **Optimized Schemas**: Write DB is normalized for transaction integrity; Read DB is denormalized and pre-indexed for single-lookup UI rendering.
- **Independent Scaling**: Read replicas or search indexes can scale to 50 nodes during peak shopping hours while the write database remains stable.
- **Resilience**: A temporary slowdown or outage in read indexing does not block customers from placing new orders.

---

## 4. Asynchronous Task Offloading and Worker Fleets

Synchronous web request threads should never execute work taking longer than 200 milliseconds. Any heavy computation must be offloaded to background workers.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Client as User Browser
    participant API as Web API Gateway
    participant Q as Task Queue (SQS / Redis)
    participant Worker as Background Worker Fleet
    participant Storage as S3 Object Store

    Client->>API: POST /export-annual-report
    API->>Q: Enqueue Job {user_id: 42, report: "2024"}
    API-->>Client: 202 Accepted {job_id: "job_987", status: "PENDING"}
    
    Note over Client: Web thread freed in 25ms. User views progress indicator.

    Q->>Worker: Consume Job
    Worker->>Worker: Generate 500-page PDF (takes 12 seconds)
    Worker->>Storage: Upload report.pdf
    Worker->>API: Publish JobComplete webhook / push notification
    API-->>Client: WebSocket Notification: Report Ready for Download
```

---

## 5. Auto-Scaling Policies and Strategies

Horizontal auto-scaling dynamically adjusts the number of active server instances to match incoming traffic demand.

### Auto-Scaling Types
1. **Target Metric Scaling**:
   - Maintains an average resource utilization target (e.g. adjust pod count to maintain 60% average CPU utilization or 1,000 active connections per node).
2. **Step Scaling**:
   - Triggers aggressive additions during sharp spikes (e.g. if CPU > 80%, add 5 nodes; if CPU > 90%, add 15 nodes).
3. **Scheduled Scaling**:
   - Pre-provisions resources ahead of known business events (e.g. scaling up 30 minutes before Super Bowl kickoff or Black Friday midnight).
4. **Predictive Scaling**:
   - Leverages historical machine learning traffic patterns to spin up instances before daily commuter spikes.

### The Scale-In Cooldown Rule
- Always configure an asymmetric cooldown period: scale out rapidly (e.g. 1-minute evaluation window) to prevent latency spikes, but scale in slowly (e.g. 10 to 15-minute cooldown) to avoid **flapping** (rapid oscillating between spinning up and destroying instances).

---

## 6. TPM Review Checklist

When auditing scalability readiness for key launches:

- [ ] Are all web application instances completely stateless?
- [ ] Has the team validated auto-scaling cooldown periods to prevent instance thrashing?
- [ ] Is long-running or CPU-intensive work offloaded to asynchronous background workers?
- [ ] Are database read-heavy workloads segregated using read replicas or CQRS patterns?
- [ ] What is the projected cloud infrastructure cost at 2x, 5x, and 10x current transaction volumes?
- [ ] Has load testing verified that horizontal scaling does not shift the bottleneck to a shared downstream database connection pool?

---

## 7. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- *The Art of Scalability: Scalable Web Architecture, Processes, and Organizations for the Modern Enterprise* (2nd Edition) by Martin L. Abbott and Michael T. Fisher (Addison-Wesley, 2015).
- **CQRS Pattern**: *CQRS* by Martin Fowler (martinfowler.com/bliki/CQRS.html, 2011).
- **Kubernetes Autoscaling**: *Horizontal Pod Autoscaler Walkthrough* (Kubernetes.io Documentation).
- *Designing Distributed Systems* by Brendan Burns (O'Reilly Media, 2018) - Chapter 4: Replicated Load-Balanced Services.


================================================================================
SECTION 14: MODULE 3 CHAPTER 2: FAULT TOLERANCE & SELF-HEALING ARCHITECTURE
FILE: 03-system-resilience-scale/02-fault-tolerance-patterns.md
================================================================================

# Module 3.2: Fault Tolerance, Resilience, and Rate Limiting

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 3: Resilience & Scale](./README.md) > **Chapter 3.2: Fault Tolerance & Rate Limiting**

---

In large distributed systems, hardware failures, network timeouts, and software bugs are not anomalies: they are guaranteed daily occurrences. Resilience is the ability of a system to gracefully degrade, isolate failures, and self-heal without cascading into a catastrophic platform outage.

---

## 1. Cascading Failures: The Anatomy of a System Collapse

A cascading failure occurs when a small, isolated issue in one component triggers failures across downstream services, ultimately bringing down the entire platform.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Issue[Database slows down from 20ms to 4000ms] --> Step1[Service B worker threads get blocked waiting for DB]
    Step1 --> Step2[Service B connection pool exhausts, memory spikes]
    Step2 --> Step3[Service A calls to Service B time out, Service A retries aggressively]
    Step3 --> Step4[Retry storm multiplies traffic by 3x on failing Service B]
    Step4 --> Crash[Complete Platform Outage]

    classDef failStyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:1px;
    class Issue,Step1,Step2,Step3,Step4,Crash failStyle;
```

---

## 2. The Circuit Breaker Pattern

Inspired by electrical circuit breakers in residential homes, this software pattern stops execution when a downstream service is struggling, allowing it time to recover.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed: Normal Operation
    
    Closed --> Open: Failure threshold exceeded (e.g. 50% errors over 10s)
    note right of Closed: Requests flow freely to downstream dependency
    
    Open --> HalfOpen: Sleep window expires (e.g. 30 seconds)
    note right of Open: All calls fail fast immediately. Fallback response returned.
    
    HalfOpen --> Closed: Canary probes succeed
    HalfOpen --> Open: Canary probe fails
    note right of HalfOpen: Limited trial requests allowed to test downstream health
```

### Circuit Breaker States Explained
1. **Closed (Normal)**: All requests flow through. If consecutive errors or latency exceed defined thresholds, the breaker trips to *Open*.
2. **Open (Failing Fast)**: All calls return immediately with a predefined fallback error or cached default response. No network traffic reaches the struggling downstream service.
3. **Half-Open (Canary Testing)**: After a configured sleep timeout, the breaker permits a small percentage of trial requests. If they succeed, it resets to *Closed*. If they fail, it trips back to *Open*.

---

## 3. Retries and Exponential Backoff with Jitter

Blindly retrying failed network requests creates a **Retry Storm** that overwhelms recovering services. Resilient systems employ exponential backoff with randomized jitter.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Attempt1[Attempt 1: Immediate failure] --> Wait1[Wait base * 2^0 = 100ms + random jitter]
    Wait1 --> Attempt2[Attempt 2: Failed]
    Attempt2 --> Wait2[Wait base * 2^1 = 200ms + random jitter]
    Wait2 --> Attempt3[Attempt 3: Failed]
    Wait3[Wait base * 2^2 = 400ms + random jitter]
    Attempt3 --> Wait3
    Wait3 --> DLQ[Max Retries Exceeded: Drop or Send to DLQ]

    classDef retryStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class Attempt1,Wait1,Attempt2,Wait2,Attempt3,Wait3,DLQ retryStyle;
```

### Why "Full Jitter" is Essential
Without jitter, thousands of clients that failed at time $T_0$ will all retry at exactly $T_0 + 100\text{ms}$, and again at $T_0 + 300\text{ms}$, creating periodic waves of destructive traffic (the thundering herd). Adding random jitter spreads retries uniformly across time.

$$\text{Sleep Time} = \text{random}(0, \; \text{min}(\text{MaxSleep}, \; \text{BaseSleep} \times 2^{\text{Attempt}}))$$

---

## 4. Rate Limiting and Throttling Algorithms

Rate limiting protects APIs against abusive scrapers, denial of service attacks, and accidental client loops.

```mermaid
graph TD
    RL[Rate Limiting Algorithms] --> TB[Token Bucket]
    RL --> LB[Leaky Bucket]
    RL --> FWC[Fixed Window Counter]
    RL --> SWC[Sliding Window Counter]

    TB -->|Feature| TB_Desc[Allows controlled bursts; refills tokens at steady rate. Used by AWS/Stripe.]
    LB -->|Feature| LB_Desc[Smooths traffic to constant steady outflow. Drops excess.]
    FWC -->|Feature| FWC_Desc[Simple reset at fixed time; vulnerable to 2x boundary bursts.]
    SWC -->|Feature| SWC_Desc[Accurate rolling window, memory efficient via Redis hashes.]

    classDef algoStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class TB,LB,FWC,SWC algoStyle;
```

### Algorithm Comparison Table

| Algorithm | Handles Bursts? | Memory Footprint | Edge Case Vulnerability | Production Standard |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Token Bucket** | Yes (up to bucket capacity) | Minimal ($O(1)$ per user: timestamp + token count) | None | Industry default (AWS API Gateway, Envoy) |
| **Leaky Bucket** | No (enforces strict constant rate) | Minimal ($O(1)$ per user: queue size) | Can delay legitimate bursty traffic | Great for outbound third-party integrations |
| **Fixed Window** | No | Ultra-low ($O(1)$: single counter) | **Boundary Burst Problem**: 2x quota allowed at boundary reset | Only for coarse non-critical quotas |
| **Sliding Window Counter** | Yes | Low (smooth approximation across adjacent windows) | Low error margin (< 0.1%) | Cloudflare, high-scale distributed APIs |

---

## 5. The Bulkhead Pattern

Named after the watertight compartments in a ship's hull: if one compartment is breached and fills with water, the ship remains afloat because the damage is isolated.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph NonIsolated [Non-Isolated Shared Thread Pool: High Risk]
        ReqA[User Auth Requests] --> PoolShared[Single Shared Thread Pool: 100 Threads]
        ReqB[Heavy PDF Export Requests] --> PoolShared
        Note over PoolShared: Slow PDF exports consume all 100 threads.<br/>Auth requests get blocked completely!
    end

    subgraph BulkheadIsolated [Bulkhead Isolation: Resilient]
        ReqA2[User Auth Requests] --> PoolA[Auth Pool: 50 Threads]
        ReqB2[Heavy PDF Export Requests] --> PoolB[Export Pool: 20 Threads]
        ReqC2[Payment Requests] --> PoolC[Payment Pool: 30 Threads]
        Note over PoolB: PDF pool maxes out; Auth and Payment remain 100% healthy.
    end

    classDef dangerStyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef safeStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class NonIsolated dangerStyle;
    class BulkheadIsolated safeStyle;
```

---

## 6. Idempotency Keys in Distributed Mutations

Network timeouts create ambiguity: when a payment request times out, did the bank process the transaction or fail before execution? If the client retries blindly, the customer may be billed twice.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as Mobile App
    participant Gateway as API Gateway
    participant Cache as Redis Idempotency Store
    participant Pay as Payment Engine

    App->>App: Generate UUID: idem_key_abc123
    App->>Gateway: POST /charge {amount: $50, key: "idem_key_abc123"}
    
    Gateway->>Cache: SETNX idem_key_abc123 "PROCESSING" EX 120s
    alt Key already exists (Duplicate Request)
        Cache-->>Gateway: Exists! Return cached outcome
        Gateway-->>App: 200 OK (Previous Cached Charge Receipt)
    else Key successfully set (First Attempt)
        Cache-->>Gateway: OK (Lock acquired)
        Gateway->>Pay: Process Credit Card Charge
        Pay-->>Gateway: Charge Success (Transaction #9988)
        Gateway->>Cache: SET idem_key_abc123 "SUCCESS: tx_9988"
        Gateway-->>App: 200 OK (Charge Receipt)
    end
```

---

## 7. TPM Review Checklist

When leading operational readiness and architecture reviews:

- [ ] Does every external synchronous network call define a strict timeout (e.g. 1000ms max)?
- [ ] Are retry mechanisms governed by exponential backoff with randomized full jitter?
- [ ] Are circuit breakers instrumented on all third-party external APIs (e.g. payment processors, SMS providers)?
- [ ] Are mutating endpoints (checkout, funds transfer) protected by distributed idempotency keys?
- [ ] Are critical microservices isolated using bulkhead patterns for thread pools and database connections?
- [ ] Has the organization conducted Chaos Engineering drills (Game Days) to validate failover behaviors under simulated stress?

---

## 8. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- *Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software* (2nd Edition) by Michael T. Nygard (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2018) - Chapters on Circuit Breakers, Bulkheads, and Timeouts.
- **Backoff and Jitter**: *Exponential Backoff And Jitter* by Marc Brooker (AWS Architecture Blog, 2015).
- **Stripe Idempotency Architecture**: *Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency* (Stripe Engineering Blog, 2017).
- *Chaos Engineering: System Resiliency in Practice* by Casey Rosenthal and Nora Jones (O'Reilly Media, 2020).

SECTION 15: MODULE 3 CHAPTER 3: NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS: SLAS, SLIS & SLOS
FILE: 03-system-resilience-scale/03-slas-slis-slos-nfrs.md

# Module 3.3: High Availability, NFRs, and Disaster Recovery

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 3: Resilience & Scale](./README.md) > **Chapter 3.3: SLAs, SLOs, SLIs & Disaster Recovery**

---

Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs) define system qualities rather than specific business features: how fast, how reliable, how secure, and how recoverable a system is. For technical program managers, mastering Service Level Objectives (SLOs), High Availability math, and Disaster Recovery (DR) models is essential for managing executive expectations and preventing contractual breach penalties.

---

## 1. The Reliability Trinity: SLI, SLO, and SLA

Program managers often confuse these three acronyms. Here is the operational hierarchy:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    SLI[SLI: Service Level Indicator<br/>What is the actual measured metric?] --> SLO[SLO: Service Level Objective<br/>What is our internal engineering target?]
    SLO --> SLA[SLA: Service Level Agreement<br/>What is our contractual promise to customers?]

    classDef tStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class SLI,SLO,SLA tStyle;
```

### Definitions and Examples

1. **SLI (Service Level Indicator)**:
   - A quantifiable metric tracking service health in real time.
   - *Example*: The percentage of successful HTTP GET requests responding in under 200ms over a rolling 30-day window.
2. **SLO (Service Level Objective)**:
   - The internal reliability target agreed upon between Product, TPM, and Engineering.
   - *Example*: 99.9% of requests must succeed with latency under 200ms over 30 days.
3. **SLA (Service Level Agreement)**:
   - The formal legal agreement with customers specifying financial or contractual consequences (e.g. service credits, refunds) if the service underperforms.
   - *Example*: If availability drops below 99.5%, customers receive a 15% billing credit.
   - *Golden Rule for TPMs*: Always keep your internal SLO stricter than your customer-facing SLA to create an operational safety buffer.

---

## 2. High Availability: The Math of "The Nines"

Availability is mathematically calculated as:

$$\text{Availability} = \frac{\text{Uptime}}{\text{Uptime} + \text{Downtime}} \times 100\%$$

Each additional "nine" of availability reduces tolerable downtime by a factor of 10, while exponentially multiplying cloud infrastructure costs and engineering overhead.

| Availability | Downtime per Year | Downtime per Month | Downtime per Day | Typical Architecture Requirement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **99% (Two Nines)** | 3.65 days | 7.31 hours | 14.4 minutes | Single instance with scheduled backups; manual recovery |
| **99.9% (Three Nines)** | 8.76 hours | 43.8 minutes | 1.44 minutes | Multi-AZ redundant instances with automated failover behind load balancer |
| **99.99% (Four Nines)** | 52.6 minutes | 4.38 minutes | 8.64 seconds | Fully automated multi-AZ active-active tier, read replicas, automated circuit breaking |
| **99.999% (Five Nines)** | 5.26 minutes | 26.3 seconds | 0.86 seconds | Multi-region active-active deployment, global anycast, automated rollouts with connection draining |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Cost[Infrastructure & Engineering Cost]
    N2[99% - $] --> N3[99.9% - $$]
    N3 --> N4[99.99% - $$$$]
    N4 --> N5[99.999% - $$$$$$$$]

    classDef costStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class N2,N3,N4,N5 costStyle;
```

---

## 3. Error Budgets and Burn Rates

An **Error Budget** is the allowable unreliability of a service over a given period:

$$\text{Error Budget} = 100\% - \text{SLO}$$

For a service with a **99.9% SLO**, the error budget is **0.1%**. Out of 10,000,000 requests per month, up to 10,000 requests are permitted to fail without breaching the objective.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph ErrorBudgetPolicy [TPM Governance: Error Budget Policy]
        EB[Monthly Error Budget Remaining] --> Check{Is Error Budget > 0%?}
        Check -->|Yes: Healthy| Green[Deploy new features, run A/B experiments, move fast]
        Check -->|No: Exhausted| Red[Feature Freeze! All engineering sprints pivot to reliability and tech debt]
    end

    classDef gStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef rStyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:1px;
    class Green gStyle;
    class Red rStyle;
```

### Burn Rate Monitoring
- **Burn Rate 1**: Consumes 100% of the monthly error budget in exactly 30 days (steady baseline).
- **Burn Rate 14.4**: Consumes 100% of the budget in 2 days. Triggers a high-priority on-call page to prevent SLA breach.

---

## 4. Disaster Recovery: RPO vs RTO

In the event of a catastrophic regional datacenter failure (e.g. power grid collapse or network severance), two metrics define the recovery strategy:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Past[Disaster Event Occurs] --> Point1[RPO: Recovery Point Objective]
    Past --> Point2[RTO: Recovery Time Objective]

    Point1 -->|Measures Data Loss| D1[How many minutes/hours of uncommitted data was lost?]
    Point2 -->|Measures Downtime| D2[How long until the system is restored and serving traffic?]

    classDef drStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class Point1,Point2,D1,D2 drStyle;
```

1. **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)**:
   - Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time backward from the outage.
   - *Example*: If RPO is 15 minutes, snapshots or replication streams must guarantee no more than 15 minutes of transactional data is lost.
2. **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)**:
   - Maximum acceptable duration of downtime required to restore normal operations.
   - *Example*: If RTO is 1 hour, the secondary infrastructure must be fully operational within 60 minutes.

---

## 5. Disaster Recovery Strategies Continuum

The choice of disaster recovery topology is a direct trade-off between RTO/RPO targets and operating expenditure.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Strategies [Disaster Recovery Strategies Continuum]
        direction LR
        S1[Backup & Restore<br/>RTO: Hours to Days<br/>RPO: 24 Hours<br/>Cost: $]
        S2[Pilot Light<br/>RTO: 1 to 2 Hours<br/>RPO: Minutes<br/>Cost: $$]
        S3[Warm Standby<br/>RTO: 5 to 15 Minutes<br/>RPO: Seconds<br/>Cost: $$$]
        S4[Multi-Region Active-Active<br/>RTO: Near Zero<br/>RPO: Zero to Sub-second<br/>Cost: $$$$$]
    end

    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4

    classDef s1Style fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#94a3b8,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef s2Style fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef s3Style fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef s4Style fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#10b981,stroke-width:2px;
    class S1 s1Style;
    class S2 s2Style;
    class S3 s3Style;
    class S4 s4Style;
```

### Strategy Breakdown

1. **Backup & Restore**:
   - Data is regularly backed up to cloud object storage (e.g. S3 Glacier) in another region.
   - In a disaster, new compute instances and databases are provisioned from scratch and restored from backup. Slowest, but lowest cost.
2. **Pilot Light**:
   - Critical core data is continuously replicated to the standby region. Core databases run at minimal spec, but application compute clusters are kept turned off.
   - In a disaster, compute clusters are provisioned via Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) and database instances are scaled up.
3. **Warm Standby**:
   - A fully functional, scaled-down duplicate environment runs continuously in the secondary region.
   - In a disaster, DNS or global load balancers redirect traffic, and the standby environment auto-scales to 100% capacity.
4. **Multi-Region Active-Active**:
   - Both regions simultaneously serve live production traffic. If Region A collapses, global traffic automatically shifts to Region B without human intervention.
   - Highest cost and operational complexity; requires distributed databases and multi-region routing.

---

## 6. TPM Review Checklist

When establishing operational standards and NFR baselines:

- [ ] Are SLIs defined around user-centric experience rather than raw server metrics?
- [ ] Is the internal SLO more restrictive than the customer SLA to provide an error buffer?
- [ ] Is an Error Budget Policy documented and signed off by Product and Engineering leaders?
- [ ] Are RPO and RTO targets explicitly documented for tier-1 critical systems?
- [ ] Has the disaster recovery failover process been tested in production within the last 12 months?
- [ ] Did the team calculate the financial ROI before committing to a 99.99% or 99.999% availability goal?

---

## 7. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- *Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems* by Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, and Niall Richard Murphy (O'Reilly Media, 2016) - Chapter 3: Embracing Risk & Chapter 4: Service Level Objectives.
- *The Site Reliability Workbook: Practical Ways to Implement SRE* by Betsy Beyer et al. (O'Reilly Media, 2018) - Chapter 2: Implementing SLOs.
- **AWS Reliability Pillar**: *AWS Well-Architected Framework: Reliability Pillar Whitepaper* (Amazon Web Services, 2023).
- **Disaster Recovery Guidance**: *Disaster Recovery of Workloads on AWS: Recovery in the Cloud* (AWS Whitepaper, 2022).

# Module 4: The TPM Execution and Architecture Framework

[Home](../README.md) > **Module 4: TPM Execution Framework**

---

## Overview

Technical Program Managers are evaluated not by their ability to write single-machine algorithms, but by their capacity to drive architectural consensus, identify critical cross-team dependencies, quantify infrastructure costs, mitigate production risks, and lead zero-downtime migrations. This module provides the operational frameworks, estimation formulas, deployment strategies, and governance standards essential for senior and principal TPM leadership.

---

## Module Learning Objectives

1. **Structured Architectural Communication**: Lead 45-minute system design reviews and interviews using a battle-tested 5-stage blueprint covering scope, high-level architecture, deep-dives, bottlenecks, and program delivery.
2. **Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Planning**: Rapidly size QPS, storage, bandwidth, and cache working sets using powers-of-two approximations and modern cloud latency numbers.
3. **Zero-Downtime Migrations**: Plan and execute legacy modernization programs using the Strangler Fig pattern, Blue-Green deployments, Canary rollouts, and dark launching.
4. **Observability & Governance**: Establish telemetry baselines using the Google SRE Four Golden Signals, OpenTelemetry distributed tracing, identity management (OAuth2/OIDC/JWT), envelope encryption, and compliance governance (GDPR, SOC 2).

---

## Chapter Directory

| Chapter | Title | Focus Areas | Key Trade-offs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **[4.1](./01-tpm-system-design-framework.md)** | The TPM System Design Framework | 5-stage interview blueprint, time allocation, anti-patterns, TPM vs SWE | Breadth vs depth, technical precision vs delivery roadmap |
| **[4.2](./02-back-of-the-envelope-math.md)** | Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Planning | Powers of 2, latency numbers, QPS, storage, bandwidth, cache sizing | Mental math approximations vs detailed capacity sizing |
| **[4.3](./03-migration-deployment-strategies.md)** | Migration & Safe Deployment Strategies | Strangler Fig, Blue-Green, Canary, Dark Launching, automated rollbacks | Release velocity vs blast-radius containment, cloud overhead |
| **[4.4](./04-observability-governance.md)** | Observability, Security & Governance | Metrics/Logs/Traces, OpenTelemetry, Four Golden Signals, OAuth2, KMS | Telemetry storage cost vs forensic depth, security vs developer friction |

---

## Suggested Prerequisites

- Completion of Modules 1 through 3.
- Familiarity with agile sprint planning, roadmaps, and cross-functional team structures.

# Module 4.1: The TPM System Design Framework

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 4: TPM Execution Framework](./README.md) > **Chapter 4.1: The TPM System Design Framework**

---

System design interviews and architecture design reviews evaluate Technical Program Managers differently than Software Engineers. While software engineers are assessed on code constructs, concurrency primitives, and algorithmic efficiency, TPMs are evaluated on **architectural breadth, trade-off evaluation, cross-functional risk mitigation, capacity planning, and project delivery roadmaps**.

---

## 1. SWE vs TPM System Design Lens

Understanding the evaluation criteria is critical for succeeding in TPM interviews at top technology firms (Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Uber).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph SWELens [Software Engineer Lens]
        direction TB
        S1[Low-level data structures]
        S2[Thread locking & memory pointers]
        S3[Algorithm time/space complexity]
        S4[Component-level implementation details]
    end

    subgraph TPMLens [Technical Program Manager Lens]
        direction TB
        T1[Cross-system architecture & boundaries]
        T2[Capacity planning & infrastructure cost]
        T3[Single points of failure & disaster recovery]
        T4[Cross-team dependencies & migration milestones]
    end

    classDef sweStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef tpmStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class SWELens sweStyle;
    class TPMLens tpmStyle;
```

---

## 2. The 5-Stage TPM System Design Blueprint

Use this structured five-stage framework to drive any 45-minute architectural interview or cross-functional architecture review.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1[Stage 1: Clarify Scope & Non-Functional Requirements<br/>5 to 7 Minutes] --> S2[Stage 2: High-Level Architecture & API Boundaries<br/>10 Minutes]
    S2 --> S3[Stage 3: Deep-Dive on Core Components & Data Model<br/>12 to 15 Minutes]
    S3 --> S4[Stage 4: Scaling, Bottlenecks & Failure Modes<br/>8 to 10 Minutes]
    S4 --> S5[Stage 5: TPM Execution Lens: Dependencies, Phasing & Cost<br/>5 Minutes]

    classDef sStyle fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#334155,stroke-width:1px;
    class S1,S2,S3,S4,S5 sStyle;
```

---

## 3. Step-by-Step Blueprint Breakdown

### Stage 1: Clarify Scope and Requirements (5 to 7 Minutes)
Never jump straight into drawing boxes. Clarify functional and non-functional requirements to set clear boundaries.

- **Functional Requirements (What the system does)**:
  - Identify 2 or 3 core use cases (e.g. "Users can upload video segments; users can stream video adaptively").
  - Explicitly state out-of-scope features (e.g. "Video comments and recommendations are out of scope for today").
- **Non-Functional Requirements (How well it performs)**:
  - Scale: Monthly active users (MAU), daily active users (DAU), read/write ratio.
  - Latency: Target p95 / p99 response times (e.g. p99 < 200ms).
  - Availability: Target "nines" (e.g. 99.99% availability).
  - Data Retention & Compliance: Data durability, GDPR, data residency constraints.

### Stage 2: High-Level Architecture (10 Minutes)
Establish the end-to-end data flow before zooming into details.

- Draw the client ingress path: Client $\rightarrow$ DNS $\rightarrow$ CDN $\rightarrow$ Load Balancer $\rightarrow$ API Gateway.
- Partition the backend into logical domain services (e.g. Ingestion Service, Processing Service, Query Service).
- Define primary data storage tiers (Transactional DB, Cache, Object Storage).
- Define core API contracts (e.g. `POST /api/v1/trips`, `GET /api/v1/drivers/nearby`).

### Stage 3: Deep-Dive and Data Modeling (12 to 15 Minutes)
Zoom in on the 1 or 2 most complex components in the design.

- **Data Model**:
  - Relational vs NoSQL selection with rationale.
  - Primary keys, foreign keys, partition keys, and secondary indexing.
- **Data Flow Mechanics**:
  - Walk through an end-to-end read and write sequence step-by-step.
  - Explain cache population, invalidation triggers, and asynchronous messaging queues.

### Stage 4: Scaling, Bottlenecks, and Failure Modes (8 to 10 Minutes)
Proactively attack your own architecture before the interviewer or team points out flaws.

- **Single Points of Failure (SPOFs)**: What happens if the load balancer, primary database, or Redis master dies?
- **Hot Partitions**: How do we handle sudden traffic surges from viral events or celebrity accounts?
- **Resilience Controls**: Where are circuit breakers, rate limiters, DLQs, and fallback mechanisms placed?

### Stage 5: The TPM Execution Lens (5 Minutes)
This stage distinguishes strong TPM candidates from engineers:

- **Cross-Team Dependencies**: Identify teams involved (e.g. Infrastructure, Security, Mobile Client, Data Platform).
- **Migration & Phasing**: How do we transition from legacy systems without downtime (Strangler Fig pattern, dark launching)?
- **Infrastructure Cost Sizing**: Rough cloud budget estimation (compute, network egress, storage tiering).
- **Launch Risks & Rollback Criteria**: Specific telemetry metrics that trigger an automated abort of the rollout.

---

## 4. Time Allocation Breakdown (45-Minute Interview)

| Stage | Activity | Time Target | Goal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Stage 1** | Scope, NFRs & Calculations | 5 to 7 mins | Eliminate ambiguity; establish agreed scale parameters |
| **Stage 2** | High-Level Architecture Diagram | 10 mins | Establish full end-to-end flow without getting bogged down |
| **Stage 3** | Component Deep-Dive & Data Model | 12 to 15 mins | Demonstrate technical depth on primary system challenges |
| **Stage 4** | Bottlenecks, Scale & Resilience | 8 to 10 mins | Prove operational durability and failure handling |
| **Stage 5** | Execution, Phasing & Trade-offs | 5 mins | Demonstrate program delivery, risk mitigation, and leadership |

---

## 5. Architectural Decision Records (ADRs)

In enterprise programs, architectural choices must be documented to prevent endless re-litigation of technical debates. A Technical Program Manager owns the ADR process:

### Standard ADR Template (Michael Nygard Format)

```markdown
# ADR-004: Adoption of Apache Kafka for Asynchronous Order Event Streaming

## Status
Accepted (Date: 2026-03-15)

## Context
Our monolithic ordering service handles 15,000 orders/minute. Post-order workflows (inventory decrement, fraud analysis, invoice PDF generation, customer email notification) are currently executed via synchronous HTTP RPC. Downstream latency spikes in the invoice generation service are causing timeout cascades and order dropouts.

## Decision
We will decouple post-order fulfillment workflows using Apache Kafka. The checkout API will commit the order record to the primary database, publish an `OrderPlaced` event to Kafka topic `orders.v1`, and return HTTP 201 immediately to the client.

## Consequences
- **Positive**: Web request latency drops from 850ms to 65ms. Downstream outages no longer block checkout.
- **Negative**: Downstream consumers require idempotency keys to handle duplicate events. Introduces operational overhead of managing Kafka broker clusters and ZooKeeper/KRaft.

## Compliance & Monitoring
Order event lag must be monitored in Datadog with an alert threshold of lag > 5,000 messages.
```

---

## 6. Worked Design Review Examples: How a Strong TPM Challenges Proposals

During architectural review boards, a TPM must evaluate proposals critically. Below are three real-world examples:

### Example 1: E-Commerce Inventory Reservation Proposal
- **Proposed Architecture**: Checkout service makes synchronous HTTP REST calls to the Inventory Service, which runs `SELECT stock FROM inventory WHERE item_id = ? FOR UPDATE` on a single PostgreSQL database.
- **Questions a Strong TPM Must Ask**:
  1. *Throughput Ceiling*: A relational row-level lock on PostgreSQL maxes out at ~2,000 writes/sec. During a flash sale of 50,000 QPS, how will this avoid connection pool exhaustion?
  2. *Blast Radius*: If the inventory service experiences a latency spike, how do we prevent checkout threads from getting exhausted and dropping cart views?
  3. *Idempotency*: If the client times out after 1,000ms while the database write actually succeeded, what prevents duplicate stock reservation on retry?

### Example 2: IoT Fleet Telemetry Ingestion Proposal
- **Proposed Architecture**: 250,000 connected vehicles ping telemetry every 5 seconds directly to an API Gateway, which inserts rows into a standard relational database with multiple secondary indexes on timestamp and vehicle ID.
- **Questions a Strong TPM Must Ask**:
  1. *Storage Engine Suitability*: Ingestion rate is 50,000 writes/sec. A B-Tree storage engine requires random disk page writes for secondary indexes. Why are we not using an LSM-Tree write-optimized engine (Cassandra or ScyllaDB) or time-series database?
  2. *Buffer Layer*: If the database undergoes a failover maintenance window for 30 seconds, where do the 1.5 million in-flight vehicle pings get buffered to prevent permanent data loss?
  3. *Retention and Cold Storage*: At 50,000 writes/sec, the database accumulates 4.3 Billion rows per day. What is the automated partitioning and cold storage tiering policy to prevent disk saturation?

### Example 3: Global User Feed Comments Proposal
- **Proposed Architecture**: Multi-region active-active relational database deployment where users in London and Tokyo write comments to local read-write database instances, replicating synchronously across the globe.
- **Questions a Strong TPM Must Ask**:
  1. *Physical Latency Bounds*: Synchronous consensus across Tokyo and London takes at least 150ms per write due to speed-of-light networking limits. Are users willing to wait 250ms+ just to post a casual comment?
  2. *CAP Theorem Alignment*: User comments are inherently tolerant of eventual consistency. Why are we paying 5x cloud infrastructure costs for synchronous cross-region consensus instead of an AP asynchronous replication model?

---

## 7. Common Anti-Patterns to Avoid

| Anti-Pattern | Description | Correction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **The Immediate Box Drawer** | Drawing diagrams before asking clarifying scale or business questions | Spend the first 5 minutes agreeing on requirements, QPS, and scope |
| **The Pure SWE Trap** | Diving deep into single-machine thread concurrency or Python code | Elevate discussion to distributed architecture, data contracts, and scaling |
| **Buzzword Stacking** | Throwing "Kafka, Redis, and Kubernetes" at every problem without justification | Explain *why* a technology fits the specific read/write access pattern |
| **Silent Architect** | Designing in complete silence without narrating thought processes | Think out loud; present trade-offs transparently: "Option A gives X but costs Y" |
| **Ignoring Operational Cost** | Proposing infinite multi-region replication for non-critical features | Highlight cost vs reliability trade-offs: "99.9% is sufficient and saves 60% cloud spend" |

---

## 8. TPM Review Checklist

Before presenting an architecture to leadership or interview panels:

- [ ] Did I clarify both functional goals and non-functional targets (SLAs, scale, latency)?
- [ ] Is my data store selection justified by specific read/write access patterns?
- [ ] Have I proactively identified the top single points of failure (SPOFs)?
- [ ] Did I outline the rollout phases, cross-team dependencies, and rollback triggers?
- [ ] Am I prepared to defend the cost implications of high availability choices?

---

## 9. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- *Software Architecture: The Hard Parts: Modern Input for Objectives, Granularity, and Coupling* by Neal Ford, Mark Richards, Pramod Sadalage, and Zhamak Dehghani (O'Reilly Media, 2021).
- **Architecture Decision Records**: *Documenting Architecture Decisions* by Michael Nygard (cognitect.com, 2011).
- *Staff Engineer: Leadership Beyond the Management Track* by Will Larson (Stripe Press, 2021) - Chapters on Technical Strategy and Architecture Reviews.


================================================================================
SECTION 18: MODULE 4 CHAPTER 2: BACK-OF-THE-ENVELOPE MATH & CAPACITY PLANNING
FILE: 04-tpm-execution-framework/02-back-of-the-envelope-math.md
