# Module 4.2: Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Planning

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 4: TPM Execution Framework](./README.md) > **Chapter 4.2: Capacity Planning & Estimation**

---

Back-of-the-envelope calculations allow technical program managers to rapidly size infrastructure, sanity-check engineering proposals, estimate annual cloud expenditures, and determine whether a proposed architecture is physically feasible before writing code.

---

## 1. The Power-of-Two and Storage Units Cheat Sheet

Memorizing these approximations enables fast mental arithmetic during architecture reviews and interviews.

| Power of 2 | Exact Value | Approximation | Unit Equivalent |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **$2^{10}$** | 1,024 | 1 Thousand ($10^3$) | 1 Kilobyte (KB) |
| **$2^{20}$** | 1,048,576 | 1 Million ($10^6$) | 1 Megabyte (MB) |
| **$2^{30}$** | 1,073,741,824 | 1 Billion ($10^9$) | 1 Gigabyte (GB) |
| **$2^{40}$** | 1,099,511,627,776 | 1 Trillion ($10^{12}$) | 1 Terabyte (TB) |
| **$2^{50}$** | 1,125,899,906,842,624 | 1 Quadrillion ($10^{15}$) | 1 Petabyte (PB) |

---

## 2. Time Conversion Approximations

| Time Horizon | Exact Seconds | Mental Math Approximation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1 Hour** | 3,600 seconds | $\approx 4,000$ seconds |
| **1 Day** | 86,400 seconds | $\approx 100,000$ seconds ($10^5$) |
| **1 Month (30 days)** | 2,592,000 seconds | $\approx 2.5 \times 10^6$ seconds |
| **1 Year** | 31,536,000 seconds | $\approx 3 \times 10^7$ seconds |

> **Mental Math Pro-Tip**: Dividing a daily figure by $10^5$ gives a fast, conservative estimate of Queries Per Second (QPS). For example, 10 million daily actions $\approx 10,000,000 / 100,000 = 100\text{ QPS}$.

---

## 3. Modern Latency Numbers Every TPM Should Know

Understanding physical hardware and networking limits prevents proposing architectures that violate latency SLAs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph NanoMicro [Nanoseconds to Microseconds: Memory & Local Disk]
        L1[L1 Cache Access: 0.5 to 1 ns]
        RAM[Main Memory RAM Access: 100 ns]
        SSD[NVMe SSD Read 4KB: 10 to 50 microseconds]
    end

    subgraph MilliSeconds [Milliseconds: Network Boundaries]
        DC[Same Datacenter Round Trip: 0.5 ms]
        IntraRegion[Cross-AZ within Same Cloud Region: 1 to 2 ms]
        TransCont[Cross-US Round Trip NY to SF: 40 ms]
        TransOcean[Transatlantic Round Trip NY to London: 80 ms]
        Global[Global Round Trip Tokyo to London: 150 to 200 ms]
    end

    NanoMicro --> MilliSeconds

    classDef nmStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef msStyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:1px;
    class NanoMicro nmStyle;
    class MilliSeconds msStyle;
```

### Core Architecture Insights
1. **Memory is roughly 1,000x faster than SSD reads**, and SSD reads are roughly 1,000x faster than traditional spinning disk seeks.
2. **Datacenter network calls take 0.5ms to 2ms**. An API that chains 10 sequential synchronous microservice calls will incur 20ms of pure network round-trip overhead before doing any compute.
3. **Cross-ocean calls are bounded by the speed of light in fiber optic cables** ($\approx 200,000\text{ km/s}$). You cannot reduce London-to-New York round-trip latency below 60ms through software optimization.

---

## 4. Step-by-Step Worked Capacity Planning Example

Scenario: Design an image-sharing platform (e.g. Instagram-lite) for **100 Million Daily Active Users (DAU)**.

### Step 1: Calculate Queries Per Second (QPS)
- Each user views an average of 20 image posts per day.
- Each user uploads an average of 1 photo per day.

$$\text{Daily Read Requests} = 100\text{M} \times 20 = 2\text{ Billion reads/day}$$

$$\text{Average Read QPS} = \frac{2,000,000,000}{86,400} \approx 23,148\text{ QPS} \approx 23,000\text{ QPS}$$

$$\text{Peak Read QPS (2x Multiplier)} = 23,000 \times 2 = \mathbf{46,000\text{ QPS}}$$

$$\text{Daily Write Requests} = 100\text{M} \times 1 = 100\text{ Million uploads/day}$$

$$\text{Average Write QPS} = \frac{100,000,000}{86,400} \approx 1,157\text{ QPS} \approx 1,150\text{ QPS}$$

$$\text{Peak Write QPS (2x Multiplier)} = 1,150 \times 2 = \mathbf{2,300\text{ QPS}}$$

### Step 2: Storage Capacity Estimation (5-Year Horizon)
- Average compressed photo size: **200 KB**.
- Metadata size per post in database (user ID, post ID, timestamp, caption, CDN media URL): **500 Bytes**.

$$\text{Daily Media Storage (Object Store)} = 100\text{M uploads} \times 200\text{ KB} = 20,000\text{ GB/day} = 20\text{ Terabytes/day}$$

$$\text{5-Year Media Storage} = 20\text{ TB/day} \times 365 \times 5 \approx \mathbf{36.5\text{ Petabytes (S3 Object Storage)}}$$

$$\text{Daily Metadata Storage (Distributed DB)} = 100\text{M} \times 500\text{ Bytes} = 50\text{ GB/day}$$

$$\text{5-Year Metadata Storage} = 50\text{ GB/day} \times 365 \times 5 \approx \mathbf{91.25\text{ Terabytes (Distributed DB)}}$$

- Accounting for 3x database replication and secondary index overhead ($1.5\times$ multiplier):
  $$\text{Total Raw Database Provisioning} = 91.25\text{ TB} \times 3 \times 1.5 \approx \mathbf{410.6\text{ Terabytes}}$$

### Step 3: Network Bandwidth Estimation
- Read bandwidth (serving photos to end users):

$$\text{Average Read Bandwidth} = \text{Average Read QPS} \times \text{Average Photo Size}$$

$$\text{Average Read Bandwidth} = 23,000\text{ QPS} \times 200\text{ KB} = 4,600,000\text{ KB/s} = 4.6\text{ GB/s}$$

$$\text{In Gigabits per second (8 bits = 1 byte)} = 4.6 \times 8 \approx \mathbf{36.8\text{ Gbps egress}}$$

$$\text{Peak Read Bandwidth (2x Multiplier)} = 36.8\text{ Gbps} \times 2 \approx \mathbf{73.6\text{ Gbps egress}}$$

- An egress rate of 73.6 Gbps cannot be served directly from application origin servers without incurring massive cloud transit fees and risking server saturation. A global Content Delivery Network (CDN) is mandatory to absorb at least 90% of this bandwidth at edge POPs.

### Step 4: Storage Tiering & Cache Sizing: Media vs Metadata

A common pitfall in system design is attempting to cache 200 KB binary image files in Redis RAM. In a production architecture:
1. **Binary Media Blobs (200 KB)** are cached in **CDN Edge POPs** on fast NVMe SSDs.
2. **Post Metadata & URLs (500 Bytes)** are cached in **Redis In-Memory RAM** for ultra-fast timeline queries.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph CDNTier [CDN Edge POP Tier: Binary Caching]
        C1[20% Hot Daily Photos = 20 Million Photos]
        C2[CDN Cache Storage: 20M * 200 KB = 4 Terabytes SSD Edge Cache]
    end

    subgraph RedisTier [Redis In-Memory Tier: Metadata Caching]
        R1[20% Hot Post Metadata Records = 20 Million Records]
        R2[Raw Metadata: 20M * 500 Bytes = 10 Gigabytes]
        R3[Redis Key Overhead: 20M * 80 Bytes = 1.6 Gigabytes]
        R4[Total Redis Working Set with 30% Headroom = 15.1 Gigabytes RAM]
    end

    classDef cdnStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef redisStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class CDNTier cdnStyle;
    class RedisTier redisStyle;
```

#### Redis In-Memory Working Set Calculation
- Total distinct active posts viewed in 24 hours: 100 Million daily uploads.
- Applying the Pareto Principle (top 20% of posts generate 80% of reads):
  $$\text{Hot Working Set Count} = 100,000,000 \times 0.20 = 20\text{ Million posts}$$
  $$\text{Raw Metadata Size} = 20,000,000 \times 500\text{ Bytes} = 10\text{ Gigabytes}$$
- Adding Redis key overhead (`dictEntry`, `robj`, jemalloc allocation padding $\approx 80\text{ bytes/key}$):
  $$\text{Key Overhead} = 20,000,000 \times 80\text{ Bytes} = 1.6\text{ Gigabytes}$$
- Adding a 30% buffer for connection memory, command buffers, and headroom:
  $$\text{Target Redis Cluster RAM} = (10\text{ GB} + 1.6\text{ GB}) \times 1.30 \approx \mathbf{15.1\text{ Gigabytes RAM}}$$
- *Conclusion*: A modest 3-node Redis cluster with 16 GB RAM per node (configured with 1 primary and 2 read replicas) easily handles the entire application metadata working set with full high availability.

---

## 5. Sensitivity Analysis for Capacity Modeling

In engineering reviews, assumptions change. A senior TPM must understand how shifts in core parameters impact infrastructure requirements:

| Variable Parameter | Baseline Assumption | High-Stress Scenario | Impact on Infrastructure |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Photo Compression Size** | 200 KB | 500 KB (High-res uncompressed) | Egress bandwidth jumps from 73.6 Gbps to 184 Gbps; CDN costs multiply 2.5x |
| **Read-to-Write Ratio** | 20:1 | 50:1 (Viral live event) | Read QPS surges from 23,000 to 57,800 QPS; requires scaling API Gateway and CDN POPs |
| **User Activity Multiplier** | 2x Peak Multiplier | 5x Peak Multiplier (Breaking news) | Peak write QPS jumps from 2,300 to 5,750 QPS; requires pre-provisioned database write capacity |
| **Media Retention Policy** | 5-Year Full Retention | 90-Day Cold Tiering | Moves 95% of S3 data to S3 Glacier Flexible, reducing cloud storage bills by up to 70% |

---

## 6. TPM Review Checklist

When validating capacity numbers in engineering proposals:

- [ ] Has the team calculated both average QPS and peak QPS (minimum 2x to 3x multiplier)?
- [ ] Is storage capacity projected for a realistic lifecycle horizon (e.g. 3 to 5 years)?
- [ ] Has storage growth accounted for replication factors and index write amplification?
- [ ] Is network egress calculated in Gbps to evaluate bandwidth costs and CDN necessity?
- [ ] Are binary media files cached at CDN edges and strictly separated from in-memory Redis metadata caches?
- [ ] Was a sensitivity analysis conducted for at least one critical traffic assumption?

---

## 7. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know**: Colin Scott's Interactive Visualization (https://colin-scott.github.io/personal_website/research/interactive_latency.html).
- **Jeff Dean's System Design Numbers**: *Building Large-Scale Distributed Systems: ACM SIGOPS Keynote* by Jeff Dean (Google, 2009).
- *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly Media, 2017) - Chapter 1: Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Systems.
- **AWS S3 Storage Classes & Pricing**: Official AWS Documentation on Lifecycle Tiering.

SECTION 19: MODULE 4 CHAPTER 3: MIGRATION & ZERO-DOWNTIME DEPLOYMENT STRATEGIES

# Module 4.3: Migration and Safe Deployment Strategies

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 4: TPM Execution Framework](./README.md) > **Chapter 4.3: Migration & Deployment Strategies**

---

Large-scale distributed systems cannot be paused for a weekend maintenance window to deploy new features or replace legacy monoliths. Technical program managers must master zero-downtime migration patterns, progressive rollouts, and blast-radius containment strategies to modernize architectures safely under full production load.

---

## 1. The Strangler Fig Pattern

Named after the tropical strangler fig tree that seeds in the upper branches of a host tree, gradually grows downward, and eventually replaces the host. In software, this pattern incrementally migrates functionalities from a legacy monolith to new microservices until the monolith can be safely decommissioned.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Phase1 [Phase 1: Intercept Ingress]
        Client1[Client] --> Proxy1[API Gateway / Facade Proxy]
        Proxy1 -->|100% Traffic| Monolith1[Legacy Monolith Application]
    end

    subgraph Phase2 [Phase 2: Strangle First Service]
        Client2[Client] --> Proxy2[API Gateway / Facade Proxy]
        Proxy2 -->|Path /api/v1/auth| Micro2[New Auth Microservice]
        Proxy2 -->|Remaining Traffic| Monolith2[Legacy Monolith Application]
    end

    subgraph Phase3 [Phase 3: Full Replacement]
        Client3[Client] --> Proxy3[API Gateway / Facade Proxy]
        Proxy3 --> MicroAuth[Auth Microservice]
        Proxy3 --> MicroOrder[Order Microservice]
        Proxy3 --> MicroPay[Payment Microservice]
        Note over Monolith3: Legacy Monolith Decommissioned!
    end

    Phase1 --> Phase2 --> Phase3

    classDef pStyle fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#334155,stroke-width:1px;
    class Phase1,Phase2,Phase3 pStyle;
```

### Strangler Fig Migration Steps
1. **Deploy Ingress Facade**: Place an API Gateway or reverse proxy directly in front of the legacy monolith.
2. **Build New Service**: Implement a single, well-bounded domain (e.g. Authentication or Notifications) as a modern standalone microservice.
3. **Route Traffic via Facade**: Update gateway routing rules to direct the specific path to the new microservice while leaving all other traffic routed to the monolith.
4. **Repeat and Sunset**: Sequentially extract domains until the monolith is an empty shell, then decommission the legacy infrastructure.

---

## 2. Production Deployment Strategies

Choosing a deployment model involves balancing risk, release speed, infrastructure cost, and rollback complexity.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph BlueGreen [Blue-Green Deployment]
        direction TB
        RouterBG[Router / Load Balancer] -->|100% Active Traffic| GreenEnv[Green Environment: v1.0 Live]
        RouterBG -.->|Zero Traffic: Staging| BlueEnv[Blue Environment: v2.0 Ready]
        Note over RouterBG: Router switches 100% traffic to Blue once verified!
    end

    subgraph Canary [Canary Deployment]
        direction TB
        RouterCanary[Router / Load Balancer] -->|95% Production Traffic| ProdEnv[Baseline Fleet: v1.0]
        RouterCanary -->|5% Sample Traffic| CanaryEnv[Canary Fleet: v2.0]
        Note over CanaryEnv: Telemetry verified for 30 mins before scaling to 100%
    end

    classDef bgStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef cnStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class BlueGreen bgStyle;
    class Canary cnStyle;
```

### Detailed Strategy Comparison

| Strategy | How It Works | Downtime Profile | Cost Overhead | Rollback Speed | Operational Failure Modes | Best Suited For |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Rolling Deployment** | Replaces old pods with new pods incrementally (e.g. 20% at a time) | Near-zero downtime (conditional on connection draining) | Zero additional compute cost | Slow (requires rolling backward pod by pod) | **Connection Drops**: Occurs if `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is too short or if DB schema is not backward compatible | Standard stateless microservice releases |
| **Blue-Green Deployment** | Provisions duplicate environment (Blue). Flips router from Green to Blue in one step | Near-zero downtime (sub-second router flip) | High (requires 2x hardware capacity during rollout) | Fast (flip router back to Green) | **State Drift**: Shared databases may diverge if v1 and v2 write incompatible schemas simultaneously | High-risk releases, major framework upgrades |
| **Canary Deployment** | Routes small fraction (e.g. 1% to 5%) of live traffic to new version to observe real-world metrics | Near-zero downtime | Minimal (1 to 2 canary instances) | Fast (drain canary routing rule) | **Session Contention**: Users bouncing between v1 and v2 experiencing inconsistent UI state | High-scale consumer platforms (Google, Meta, Netflix) |
| **Shadow / Dark Launch** | Duplicates production requests to new service asynchronously without returning result to user | Zero user-visible downtime | Medium (requires duplicate compute capacity) | N/A (no live user impact) | **Side-Effect Duplication**: If shadow service inadvertently sends real emails or charges credit cards | Algorithmic rewrites, pricing engine overhauls |

---

## 3. Shadow Traffic (Dark Launching)

When rewriting critical backend pipelines (such as a search ranking algorithm or billing calculator), synthetic tests cannot replicate real-world production nuances.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Client as User Client
    participant GW as API Gateway / Proxy
    participant Prod as Production Engine (v1.0)
    participant Shadow as Shadow Engine (v2.0)
    participant Compare as Comparator / Diff Service

    Client->>GW: POST /calculate-pricing
    GW->>Prod: 1. Send Request (Synchronous)
    GW--)Shadow: 2. Duplicate Request (Asynchronous Fire-and-Forget)
    
    Prod-->>GW: Return Result: $49.99
    GW-->>Client: 200 OK: $49.99 (User latency unaffected)

    Shadow-->>Compare: Shadow Result: $49.98
    Prod-->>Compare: Production Result: $49.99
    Note over Compare: Record Discrepancy (1 cent difference) in Analytics DB
```

- **Safety**: End users never see shadow responses or errors.
- **Validation**: Program managers and engineers can run shadow traffic for weeks until the comparator reports 99.999% parity between old and new engines.

---

## 4. Feature Flags: Decoupling Deployment from Release

Traditional teams equate *deploying code to servers* with *releasing features to customers*. Feature flagging decouples these operations:

$$\text{Deployment (Technical Operation)} \neq \text{Release (Business Decision)}$$

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CodeDeployed[Code Merged & Deployed to 100% Fleet] --> CheckFlag{Feature Flag State in Redis / LaunchDarkly}
    
    CheckFlag -->|User is Internal Staff| V2_On[Show New Experience]
    CheckFlag -->|User in 10% Beta Cohort| V2_On
    CheckFlag -->|General Public| V1_Default[Show Old Experience]

    classDef flagStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class CheckFlag,V2_On,V1_Default flagStyle;
```

### TPM Benefits of Feature Flags
1. **Kill Switches**: If a newly released feature causes an error spike, turn off the flag in 500 milliseconds without deploying code or executing a rollback.
2. **Targeted Beta Testing**: Roll out features exclusively to internal employees (`@company.com`), beta users, or specific geographic regions.
3. **Trunk-Based Development**: Engineers continuously merge small code snippets into the main branch behind a disabled flag, eliminating massive, painful merge conflicts.

---

## 5. Blast Radius Control and Automated Rollback Criteria

A safe migration program must establish clear, automated rollback thresholds before initiating traffic shifts.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CanaryTraffic[Canary Traffic Shift: 5%] --> Monitor[Automated Telemetry Monitor: 15-Minute Window]
    
    Monitor --> Check1{HTTP 5xx Error Rate > 0.5%?}
    Monitor --> Check2{p99 Latency increases > 20%?}
    Monitor --> Check3{Unhandled Exceptions spike?}

    Check1 -->|Any Check Violates| AutoAbort[Automated Abort & Rollback: Zero Traffic to Canary]
    Check2 -->|Any Check Violates| AutoAbort
    Check3 -->|Any Check Violates| AutoAbort

    Check1 & Check2 & Check3 -->|All Green| Advance[Advance Traffic to Next Stage: 25%]

    classDef failStyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef passStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class AutoAbort failStyle;
    class Advance passStyle;
```

---

## 6. TPM Review Checklist

When building migration roadmaps and deployment plans:

- [ ] Has the team selected a migration strategy (Strangler Fig, Blue-Green, or Canary) suited to the risk profile?
- [ ] Are automated rollback criteria defined with quantitative SLI thresholds?
- [ ] Can the deployment roll back in under 60 seconds without requiring a cold restart?
- [ ] Are feature flags guarded by fallback defaults if the configuration service fails?
- [ ] Has the cutover runbook been peer-reviewed with named owners for each step?
- [ ] Did the team test backward compatibility of database schemas with both old and new code versions?

---

## 7. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **Strangler Fig Pattern**: *Strangler Fig Application* by Martin Fowler (martinfowler.com/bliki/StranglerFigApplication.html, 2004).
- *Continuous Delivery: Reliable Software Releases through Build, Test, and Deployment Automation* by Jez Humble and David Farley (Addison-Wesley, 2010).
- **Canary Releases**: *CanaryRelease* by Martin Fowler (martinfowler.com/bliki/CanaryRelease.html, 2014).
- **Google SRE Release Engineering**: *Site Reliability Engineering* (O'Reilly, 2016) - Chapter 8: Release Engineering.


================================================================================
SECTION 20: MODULE 4 CHAPTER 4: OBSERVABILITY, GOVERNANCE & TELEMETRY
FILE: 04-tpm-execution-framework/04-observability-governance.md

# Module 4.4: Observability, Security, and Governance

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 4: TPM Execution Framework](./README.md) > **Chapter 4.4: Observability, Security & Governance**

---

Building a scalable system is only half the battle; operating it reliably, securing user data, and maintaining regulatory compliance are what protect an organization from reputational damage and catastrophic financial fines. For technical program managers, observability and security governance are primary operational deliverables.

---

## 1. Monitoring vs Observability

- **Monitoring**: Tells you *that* a system is broken (e.g. "Error rate is 8%"). Focuses on known knowns and predefined threshold alerts.
- **Observability**: Allows you to infer the internal state of a system based on its external outputs. It enables you to diagnose *why* a system is broken during novel, unprecedented failure states (unknown unknowns).

---

## 2. The Three Pillars of Observability

Modern distributed systems rely on three telemetry data types to provide complete visibility.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Pillars [The Three Telemetry Pillars]
        P1[Metrics: Time-Series Numerical Data<br/>Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch]
        P2[Logs: Structured Event Records<br/>Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Loki]
        P3[Distributed Traces: Request Lifecycles<br/>Jaeger, OpenTelemetry, Zipkin]
    end

    P1 -->|Alerts on Anomalies| P2
    P2 -->|Finds Specific Errors| P3
    P3 -->|Pinpoints Microservice Bottleneck| RCA[Root Cause Analysis]

    classDef pilStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class P1,P2,P3 pilStyle;
```

### Pillar Comparison

| Telemetry Type | What It Measures | Storage Cost | Strengths | Weaknesses |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Metrics** | Aggregated numbers over time (e.g. CPU %, QPS, p99 latency) | Low (constant size aggregation) | Ultra-fast dashboarding and automated alerting | Lacks individual request context; cannot pinpoint specific user ID |
| **Logs** | Structured text records of discrete events (e.g. JSON log entries) | High (proportional to traffic volume) | Rich context, stack traces, and local debug information | Expensive to index; high query latency across billions of rows |
| **Traces** | End-to-end journey of a single request across multiple microservices | Medium (managed via adaptive sampling) | Identifies exact downstream hop causing latency spikes | Requires instrumenting every service with context propagation headers |

---

## 3. Distributed Tracing and OpenTelemetry (OTel)

When a single user click triggers calls across 15 microservices, traditional server logs cannot correlate the chain of events. Distributed tracing injects a unique **Trace ID** at the API gateway and propagates it across every downstream RPC call.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Client
    participant GW as API Gateway (Trace ID: abc-123)
    participant Auth as Auth Service (Span: auth-span)
    participant Order as Order Service (Span: order-span)
    participant DB as Postgres DB (Span: db-query)

    Client->>GW: POST /orders
    Note over GW: Generate Trace ID: abc-123, Parent Span ID: null
    GW->>Auth: Verify Token (Header: traceparent=abc-123;span=auth-01)
    Auth-->>GW: OK (20ms)
    GW->>Order: Create Order (Header: traceparent=abc-123;span=order-01)
    Order->>DB: INSERT into orders (Span: db-01)
    Note over DB: High Lock Contention! Latency = 850ms
    DB-->>Order: Committed
    Order-->>GW: Order Created
    GW-->>Client: 201 Created (Total Latency: 890ms)
```

- **Span**: A single unit of work (e.g. an HTTP call or database query) with a start time, duration, and metadata tags.
- **Trace**: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) of spans representing the end-to-end request.
- **OpenTelemetry (OTel)**: The vendor-neutral CNCF industry standard framework for collecting metrics, logs, and traces.

---

## 4. The Google SRE Four Golden Signals

Every production service should monitor these four foundational metrics:

```mermaid
graph LR
    GS[The Four Golden Signals] --> L[1. Latency: Time to service request]
    GS --> T[2. Traffic: Demand on system e.g. QPS]
    GS --> E[3. Errors: Rate of requests that fail]
    GS --> S[4. Saturation: Constrained resource fullness %]

    classDef sigStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class L,T,E,S sigStyle;
```

1. **Latency**: Differentiate between the latency of successful requests and failed requests (a fast 500 error is not a good response).
2. **Traffic**: Measures current throughput (e.g. HTTP requests/sec or network I/O per second).
3. **Errors**: Tracks explicit failures (HTTP 500s) and implicit failures (HTTP 200 containing error message).
4. **Saturation**: Tracks how close the system is to capacity (e.g. memory at 85%, thread pool 90% utilized).

---

## 5. Security & Identity Governance for TPMs

Security architecture spans identity management, network segmentation, and data encryption.

### Authentication (AuthN) vs Authorization (AuthZ)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Request[Incoming Request] --> AuthN{Authentication: Who are you?}
    AuthN -->|Valid Identity: User #42| AuthZ{Authorization: What can you do?}
    AuthN -->|Invalid / Expired Token| Reject401[401 Unauthorized]
    
    AuthZ -->|Allowed: Has 'admin' role| Process[Execute Operation]
    AuthZ -->|Denied: Lacks permission| Reject403[403 Forbidden]

    classDef checkStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef failStyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:1px;
    class AuthN,AuthZ checkStyle;
    class Reject401,Reject403 failStyle;
```

### Modern Authentication Standards

- **OAuth 2.0**: The authorization delegation framework allowing third parties to access user resources without passwords.
- **OpenID Connect (OIDC)**: An identity layer built directly on top of OAuth 2.0 providing federated single sign-on (SSO).
- **JSON Web Tokens (JWT)**: Cryptographically signed tokens (using HMAC or RSA/ECDSA) containing user claims and expiration timestamps.
- **RBAC vs ABAC**:
  - *RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)*: Permissions assigned to roles (e.g. Admin, Editor, Viewer).
  - *ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control)*: Permissions evaluated dynamically on attributes (e.g. "Allow access if user department is Sales AND current location is USA AND time is during business hours").

---

## 6. Data Encryption and Regulatory Compliance

| Compliance Domain | Primary Requirements | Engineering Implementation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Encryption in Transit** | Protect data traveling across networks | TLS 1.3 encryption on all public endpoints and internal mTLS (Mutual TLS) between microservices |
| **Encryption at Rest** | Protect physical hard drives and databases against theft | AES-256 encryption. Envelope encryption using Key Management Services (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS) |
| **GDPR (Right to be Forgotten)** | Ability to purge all personally identifiable information (PII) upon user request | Crypto-shredding: Encrypt user PII with an individual unique key. To "forget" the user, delete their key |
| **Data Residency** | Legal mandates requiring citizen data to remain inside national borders | Regional VPC partitioning, geolocation-based DNS routing, localized database shards |
| **SOC 2 Type II** | Continuous verification of security, availability, and confidential controls | Immutable audit logging, automated vulnerability scanning, least-privilege IAM policies |

---

## 7. TPM Review Checklist

When leading security and observability architecture sign-offs:

- [ ] Does every microservice emit the Four Golden Signals (Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation)?
- [ ] Is distributed tracing instrumented with W3C traceparent headers across all network boundaries?
- [ ] Are PII and sensitive credentials excluded from application log streams?
- [ ] Is data encrypted in transit using TLS 1.3 and at rest using KMS-managed envelope encryption?
- [ ] Is the Principle of Least Privilege enforced on all cloud IAM roles and service accounts?
- [ ] Does the design satisfy legal compliance mandates (GDPR, SOC 2, HIPAA) regarding data retention and residency?

---

## 8. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- *Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems* (O'Reilly, 2016) - Chapter 6: Monitoring Distributed Systems.
- **OpenTelemetry Specification**: OpenTelemetry Documentation and W3C Trace Context Specification (https://opentelemetry.io/).
- **RFC 6749**: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework (IETF, 2012).
- **RFC 7519**: JSON Web Token (JWT) (IETF, 2015).
- **NIST Special Publication 800-57**: *Recommendation for Key Management* (NIST, 2020).

# Module 5: Real-World Architecture Case Studies

[Home](../README.md) > **Module 5: Real-World Case Studies**

---

## Overview

Theoretical knowledge becomes actionable only when applied to complex, high-scale, end-to-end architectures. This module presents five comprehensive production case studies designed to reflect the real-world interview scenarios and engineering challenges encountered at leading technology companies (Google, Meta, Amazon, Apple, Uber, Netflix).

Each case study follows a rigorous, uniform 14-section architectural framework: from initial functional scoping and mathematical capacity planning to concrete API contracts, data models, alternative trade-off tables, failure-mode matrices, and worked TPM delivery plans.

---

## Case Study Directory

| Case Study | Title | Real-World Analog | Core Architectural Challenges |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **[5.1](./01-url-shortener.md)** | Global URL Shortener | TinyURL / Bitly | Key Generation Service (KGS), Base62 hashing, 301 vs 302 redirects, Zipfian cache sizing, abuse detection |
| **[5.2](./02-notification-engine.md)** | Multi-Channel Notification Platform | Twilio / OneSignal | Priority queue isolation, user preferences & quiet hours, vendor circuit breakers, SMS-to-push cost cascades |
| **[5.3](./03-video-streaming-platform.md)** | Global Video Streaming Platform | YouTube / Netflix | Chunked DAG GPU transcoding, Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (HLS/DASH), multi-terabit CDN egress, ISP edge caching |
| **[5.4](./04-ride-sharing-dispatch.md)** | Real-Time Ride-Sharing Dispatch | Uber / Lyft | 1.25M location pings/sec, Uber H3 hexagonal spatial indexing, distributed driver locking, WebSocket lifecycles |
| **[5.5](./05-distributed-ecommerce-checkout.md)** | Flash Sale & Distributed Checkout | Amazon / Shopify | Atomic in-memory inventory reservation (Redis Lua), Saga pattern rollback, payment idempotency, virtual waiting room |

---

## Recommended Study Approach

1. **Step 1: Attempt the Scoping First**: Before reading the solution, spend 5 minutes jotting down your own functional requirements, out-of-scope boundaries, and capacity math.
2. **Step 2: Compare Architectural Trade-offs**: Pay close attention to the Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) and why common alternative approaches were rejected.
3. **Step 3: Study the Failure Matrices**: Understand how each system behaves during partial network outages, broker crashes, or downstream vendor failures.
4. **Step 4: Practice the Interview Questions**: Attempt the practice questions at the end of each chapter under timed 10-minute conditions before reviewing the model rubric answers.

SECTION 22: CASE STUDY 1: HIGH-THROUGHPUT URL SHORTENER
FILE: 05-real-world-case-studies/01-url-shortener.md
================================================================================

# Case Study 1: Global URL Shortener (TinyURL / Bitly)

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 5: Real-World Case Studies](./README.md) > **Case Study 5.1: URL Shortener**

---

## 1. Problem Statement and Scope

A URL shortener converts long URLs into compact aliases (e.g. `https://tiny.url/x7k9p2`) and redirects incoming client requests to the original destination. While conceptually straightforward, operating this service at internet scale requires handling massive read-to-write skews, sub-15ms redirection latencies, global high availability, and phishing abuse prevention.

### In-Scope Functional Capabilities
- Shortening long URLs into unique 7-character Base62 aliases.
- Redirecting incoming requests with HTTP 302/307 status codes.
- Custom alias support (e.g. `https://tiny.url/tpm-handbook`).
- URL expiration via configurable Time-to-Live (TTL).
- Click telemetry tracking (click count, referrer, timestamp, geographic country).

### Out-of-Scope (Explicit Boundaries)
- Private enterprise vanity domains (custom DNS CNAME onboarding).
- Deep link routing into native iOS/Android mobile apps (Universal Links).
- Real-time user billing and paid subscription tiers.

---

## 2. Requirements and SLAs

### Functional Requirements
1. **Alias Generation**: System accepts a valid URL and returns a unique 7-character alias.
2. **Redirection**: System redirects incoming alias requests to the original destination in under 15ms.
3. **Collision Resistance**: System must never assign the same alias to two different long URLs while active.

### Non-Functional Requirements & SLAs
- **Availability Target**: **99.99% Uptime** (Maximum allowable downtime: 52.6 minutes/year).
- **Latency SLO**: p99 redirection latency $< 15\text{ms}$; p99 alias creation $< 100\text{ms}$.
- **Durability**: 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability for URL mapping records.
- **Read-to-Write Ratio**: High read-heavy workload estimated between 50:1 and 100:1.

---

## 3. Capacity Planning and Calculations

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    W[500M New URLs / Month<br/>Average Write QPS: 193<br/>Peak Write QPS: 386] --> Ratio[100:1 Read-to-Write Ratio]
    Ratio --> R[50 Billion Clicks / Month<br/>Average Read QPS: 19,290<br/>Peak Read QPS: 38,580]

    classDef mathStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class W,Ratio,R mathStyle;
```

### Traffic Estimates
- **New URLs Created**: 500 Million per month.
- **Average Write QPS**:
  $$\text{Write QPS} = \frac{500,000,000}{2,592,000\text{ seconds/month}} \approx \mathbf{193\text{ writes/sec}}$$
- **Peak Write QPS (2x Multiplier)**: $193 \times 2 \approx \mathbf{386\text{ writes/sec}}$.
- **Redirection Traffic (100:1 Ratio)**: 50 Billion clicks per month.
- **Average Read QPS**:
  $$\text{Read QPS} = \frac{50,000,000,000}{2,592,000\text{ seconds/month}} \approx \mathbf{19,290\text{ reads/sec}}$$
- **Peak Read QPS (2x Multiplier)**: $19,290 \times 2 \approx \mathbf{38,580\text{ reads/sec}}$.

### Storage Sizing (5-Year Horizon)
- Total URLs created over 5 years: $500\text{M/month} \times 12 \times 5 = \mathbf{30\text{ Billion records}}$.
- Data record breakdown:
  - `short_key`: 7 bytes (ASCII)
  - `original_url`: 500 bytes (average)
  - `user_id`: 16 bytes (UUID)
  - `created_at`: 8 bytes (Unix timestamp)
  - `expires_at`: 8 bytes (Unix timestamp)
  - Structural metadata and BSON/DynamoDB attribute overhead: $\approx 60\text{ bytes}$
  - **Total Record Size**: $\approx \mathbf{600\text{ bytes}}$.
- **Total Raw 5-Year Database Storage**:
  $$\text{Storage} = 30\text{ Billion} \times 600\text{ bytes} = 18,000,000,000\text{ KB} = \mathbf{18\text{ Terabytes}}$$
- Accounting for 3x multi-AZ replication and secondary index storage ($1.5\times$ factor):
  $$\text{Provisioned Storage} = 18\text{ TB} \times 3 \times 1.5 \approx \mathbf{81\text{ Terabytes}}$$

### Network Bandwidth Sizing
- **Read Ingress**: Negligible (HTTP GET headers $\approx 500\text{ bytes}$ per click $\times 19,290\text{ QPS} \approx 9.6\text{ MB/s}$).
- **Read Egress (HTTP 302 Header)**:
  $$\text{Egress Bandwidth} = 19,290\text{ QPS} \times 600\text{ bytes} \approx 11.57\text{ MB/s} = \mathbf{92.6\text{ Mbps}}$$
  $$\text{Peak Read Egress} = 92.6\text{ Mbps} \times 2 \approx \mathbf{185.2\text{ Mbps}}$$

### Cache Working Set Sizing (Zipfian Power-Law Distribution)
Clicks on shortened links follow a steep power-law (Zipfian) distribution: a small subset of viral links accounts for the vast majority of clicks.
- Rather than assuming 20% of all monthly clicks are distinct URLs, real-world telemetry shows that approximately **10 Million unique URLs** represent the active working set across any 24-hour window.
- **Raw Cache Data**: $10,000,000\text{ keys} \times 600\text{ bytes} = 6\text{ GB}$.
- **Redis Overhead**: Each key incurs $\approx 80\text{ bytes}$ (`robj`, `dictEntry`, jemalloc alignment):
  $$\text{Overhead} = 10,000,000 \times 80\text{ bytes} = 800\text{ MB}$$
- **Total Working Set with 30% Headroom**:
  $$\text{Cache RAM} = (6\text{ GB} + 0.8\text{ GB}) \times 1.30 \approx \mathbf{8.84\text{ GB RAM}}$$
- **Provisioned Cache Architecture**: A 3-shard Redis Cluster, each shard configured with 1 Primary (8 GB) and 1 Replica in an alternate Availability Zone (Total: 6 nodes of `cache.r6g.large`).

### Sensitivity Analysis
| Variable | Baseline | High Stress | Impact on Architecture |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Read Ratio** | 100:1 (38.5k peak QPS) | 500:1 (193k peak QPS) | Read tier requires scale-out of Redis cluster to 10 shards and CDN edge caching |
| **Average URL Length** | 500 bytes | 2,048 bytes (Max RFC) | Storage jumps from 18 TB to 61 TB; cache memory requirement jumps from 8.8 GB to 27 GB |

---

## 4. End-to-End System Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    User[Client Browser / Mobile App] --> DNS[Route 53 Latency-Based DNS]
    DNS --> CDN[Cloudflare Edge CDN]
    CDN -->|Cache Hit: Return 302| User
    CDN -->|Cache Miss: Forward Request| ALB[AWS Application Load Balancer]
    
    ALB --> WebFleet[URL Redirection & Shortening Service Pods]
    
    WebFleet <--> RedisCluster[(Redis Cluster: Hot URL Mappings)]
    WebFleet <--> KGS[Key Generation Service]
    WebFleet --> PrimaryDB[(NoSQL Store: Amazon DynamoDB)]
    
    WebFleet --> KafkaClickStream[(Kafka: clickstream.events)]
    KafkaClickStream --> AnalyticsWorker[Click Analytics Workers]
    AnalyticsWorker --> ClickHouseDB[(OLAP DB: ClickHouse)]

    classDef cdnStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef dbStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef appStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class CDN,RedisCluster cdnStyle;
    class PrimaryDB,ClickHouseDB dbStyle;
    class WebFleet,KGS,AnalyticsWorker appStyle;
```

---

## 5. API Contracts and Core Data Model

### API Contracts

#### 1. Create Shortened URL
- **Endpoint**: `POST /api/v1/urls`
- **Headers**:
  - `Content-Type: application/json`
  - `Idempotency-Key: <UUID>` (Client-generated UUID to prevent duplicate aliases on retry)
- **Request Payload**:
  ```json
  {
    "original_url": "https://www.example.com/products/electronics/item-98214?ref=campaign",
    "custom_alias": "spring-sale-2026",
    "ttl_days": 90
  }
  ```
- **Response Payload (HTTP 201 Created)**:
  ```json
  {
    "short_code": "spring-sale-2026",
    "short_url": "https://tiny.url/spring-sale-2026",
    "original_url": "https://www.example.com/products/electronics/item-98214?ref=campaign",
    "created_at": "2026-10-19T14:00:00Z",
    "expires_at": "2027-01-17T14:00:00Z"
  }
  ```
- **Error Codes**: `400 Bad Request` (Invalid URL), `409 Conflict` (Custom alias already in use), `429 Too Many Requests`.

#### 2. Redirect Short URL
- **Endpoint**: `GET /{short_code}`
- **Response**: `HTTP 302 Found` (or `307 Temporary Redirect`)
- **Headers**:
  - `Location: https://www.example.com/products/...`
  - `Cache-Control: private, max-age=300`

### Core Data Model (Amazon DynamoDB)

Table Name: `url_mappings`

| Attribute Name | Data Type | Key Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `short_code` | String | **Partition Key (PK)** | Unique 7-character Base62 string (e.g. `"x7k9p2"`) |
| `original_url` | String | Standard | Destination long URL (max 2,048 chars) |
| `account_id` | String | Standard | Creator account UUID |
| `created_at` | Number | Standard | Unix epoch timestamp in seconds |
| `expires_at` | Number | **TTL Attribute** | Unix epoch timestamp. DynamoDB native TTL auto-deletes expired records |
| `click_count` | Number | Standard | Coarse counter updated asynchronously |

Global Secondary Index (GSI): `account_id-created_at-index`
- **PK**: `account_id`
- **Sort Key (SK)**: `created_at`
- **Purpose**: Enables rapid retrieval of all links created by a specific user account.

---

## 6. Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) and Alternatives

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Alt1 [Alternative 1: Hash of Long URL + Collision Loop]
        A1[Compute SHA-256 of URL] --> A2[Encode in Base62 & Truncate to 7 Chars]
        A2 --> A3{Check DB: Collision?}
        A3 -->|Yes| A4[Append Salt & Hash Again: High Latency Penalty]
        A3 -->|No| A5[Commit to DB]
    end

    subgraph Alt2 [Alternative 2: Centralized Key Generation Service - Recommended]
        B1[Offline Worker pre-generates unique 7-char random strings]
        B1 --> B2[(Key Depot Database: Unused vs Used Tables)]
        B2 --> B3[KGS Servers load 50,000 keys into local memory]
        B3 --> B4[App Server requests pre-minted unique key in O 1 time]
    end

    classDef badStyle fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef goodStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    class Alt1 badStyle;
    class Alt2 goodStyle;
```

### Architectural Comparison Matrix

| Criteria | Alternative 1: SHA-256 Hash + Retry | Alternative 2: Key Generation Service (KGS) | Alternative 3: Distributed ID + Base62 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Write Latency** | Variable (15ms to 250ms during collision retries) | **Sub-millisecond** ($O(1)$ in-memory assignment) | Fast (1ms to 5ms via Snowflake generator) |
| **Collision Probability** | Moderate (birthday paradox increases as table fills) | **Zero runtime collisions** (pre-deduplicated) | Zero (Snowflake IDs are globally unique) |
| **Predictability** | Poor (collision loops consume unpredictable DB IOPS) | **Deterministic** | Deterministic |
| **Security Risk** | Low | Low | Sequential Snowflake IDs allow scrapers to guess URLs |
| **Operational Complexity** | Low (no extra services) | Moderate (requires managing KGS fleet & ZooKeeper) | Moderate (requires clock-drift synchronized daemons) |

### Decision Outcome
**Adopt Alternative 2 (Key Generation Service)**. KGS provides predictable, sub-millisecond write latency, completely decouples key generation from user web requests, and guarantees zero runtime database collision checks.

### Boundary Conditions: When KGS is No Longer Appropriate
If the application shifts from public web shortening to an internal microservice generating short IDs for billions of ephemeral background tasks, the operational overhead of KGS exceeds its value; a local 64-bit distributed Snowflake generator becomes the superior choice.

---

## 7. Failure-Mode and Recovery Matrix (FMEA)

| Failure Scenario | Detection Mechanism | Immediate System Behavior | Automated Recovery | Manual Runbook Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Redis Node Crash** | Sentinel / Cluster heartbeat timeout (> 3s) | Read requests temporarily fall back to read replica or DynamoDB | Redis Cluster promotes replica to primary in under 5 seconds | Verify replica promotion in Datadog; check replication lag |
| **KGS Server Instance Crash** | Kubernetes liveness probe failure | In-memory keys assigned to that pod (up to 50k keys) remain marked `UNUSED` or are lost | Kubernetes provisions replacement pod; pulls new unallocated key range | If unallocated keys run low (< 5M), trigger manual batch generation script |
| **DynamoDB Throttle Spike** | CloudWatch `ReadThrottleEvents` metric alarm | Client experiences p99 latency spike to 200ms | Exponential backoff with jitter on app client; Redis absorbs 95% reads | Increase provisioned read capacity units (RCU) or enable auto-scaling |
| **Analytics Kafka Topic Stalled** | Consumer lag metric exceeds 100,000 messages | Redirections continue normally (click tracking is decoupled) | Kafka consumer auto-scaling group adds 5 worker pods | Inspect ClickHouse ingestion cluster for slow batch inserts |

---

## 8. Security, Abuse Prevention, and Governance

1. **Malicious Link & Phishing Detection**:
   - Newly submitted URLs are asynchronously scanned against the Google Safe Browsing API and PhishTank before the alias is activated.
   - High-risk domains (e.g. newly registered TLDs) are placed in a quarantined state pending heuristic analysis.
2. **Rate Limiting at Edge**:
   - Enforce a limit of 100 URL shortening creations per IP per hour using Redis token buckets at the API Gateway.
   - Public redirection endpoints are rate-limited to 1,000 requests/minute per source IP to prevent automated scrapers from enumerating short codes.
3. **Data Privacy**:
   - IP addresses collected in click telemetry are anonymized (last octet stripped) to maintain strict compliance with GDPR regulations.

---

## 9. Observability and Monitoring Thresholds

| Metric Name | Telemetry Type | Target SLA / Baseline | P1 Critical Alert Threshold |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Redirection Latency (p99)** | Metric (Histogram) | $< 15\text{ms}$ | $> 50\text{ms}$ for 3 consecutive minutes |
| **HTTP 5xx Error Rate** | Metric (Counter) | $< 0.01\%$ | $> 0.1\%$ over 1-minute window |
| **Cache Hit Ratio (CHR)** | Metric (Gauge) | $> 90\%$ | $< 80\%$ (Indicates cache eviction storm) |
| **KGS Unallocated Key Pool** | Metric (Gauge) | $> 50,000,000$ | $< 5,000,000$ (Trigger batch key generator) |

---

## 10. Migration, Launch Gates, and TPM Execution Plan

### Phased Rollout Schedule

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Phase1[Phase 1: Shadow Launch<br/>Mirror 5% live read traffic to validate KGS latency] --> Phase2[Phase 2: Internal Canary<br/>Route internal employees to new shortening engine]
    Phase2 --> Phase3[Phase 3: Public Canary<br/>5% public traffic routed via weighted Route 53 DNS]
    Phase3 --> Phase4[Phase 4: Full Cutover<br/>100% traffic on new architecture; decommission legacy]

    classDef pStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class Phase1,Phase2,Phase3,Phase4 pStyle;
```

### RACI Matrix

| Workstream Deliverable | Engineering Lead | Senior TPM | Security Architect | SRE / Ops |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **KGS Engine Implementation** | **Accountable** | Consulted | Informed | Informed |
| **Phishing Abuse Scanner** | Responsible | Consulted | **Accountable** | Informed |
| **Capacity Sizing & Cost Approval** | Consulted | **Accountable** | Informed | Responsible |
| **Canary Traffic Rollout Execution** | Responsible | **Accountable** | Informed | Responsible |

### Automated Rollback Triggers
- Automatic rollback occurs within 60 seconds if HTTP 5xx error rate exceeds 0.2% or p99 latency exceeds 60ms during any canary stage.

---

## 11. Practice System Design Questions and Model Answers

### Question 1: Why use HTTP 302 Found instead of HTTP 301 Moved Permanently?
**Model Answer**:
HTTP 301 tells client browsers to cache the redirection permanently on local disk. While this minimizes origin server load, subsequent clicks from the same user device bypass our infrastructure completely, making it impossible to capture click counts, referrer data, or geolocation analytics. HTTP 302 (or HTTP 307) forces the client to query our edge/origin on every click, preserving real-time analytics integrity.

### Question 2: How would you prevent a distributed race condition if two KGS instances pull the same key range?
**Model Answer**:
We isolate key ranges in the database using optimistic concurrency control or distributed consensus (Apache ZooKeeper / etcd). When a KGS pod requests a new block of 50,000 keys, it executes an atomic conditional update: `UPDATE key_depot SET status = 'ASSIGNED', assigned_to = 'kgs_pod_04' WHERE range_id = 12 AND status = 'AVAILABLE'`. If two pods attempt to claim range 12 simultaneously, one fails and retries range 13.

---

## 12. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly Media, 2017) - Chapter 7: Transactions & Distributed Locking.
- **Base62 Encoding Standard**: RFC 4648 (The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings).
- **Amazon DynamoDB Architecture Guide**: Best Practices for Designing Partition Keys (AWS Documentation).

SECTION 23: CASE STUDY 2: MULTI-CHANNEL NOTIFICATION ENGINE

# Case Study 2: Scalable Multi-Channel Notification Engine

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 5: Real-World Case Studies](./README.md) > **Case Study 5.2: Notification Engine**

---

## 1. Problem Statement and Scope

A global notification platform delivers transactional and promotional messages across multiple channels: Mobile Push (Apple APNs, Google FCM), SMS (Twilio, Sinch, AWS SNS), and Email (SendGrid, AWS SES). For a Technical Program Manager, this system involves priority queuing, downstream third-party vendor management, customer quiet-hour compliance, and significant cost optimization.

### In-Scope Functional Capabilities
- Multi-channel delivery (iOS Push, Android Push, SMS, Email).
- Strict priority tiers (P0 urgent OTPs, P1 transactional, P2 bulk marketing).
- User notification preferences, channel opt-outs, and quiet-hour scheduling.
- Automated vendor circuit breaking and fallback routing.
- End-to-end delivery tracking across discrete lifecycle states: `ATTEMPTED`, `ACCEPTED`, `DELIVERED`, `FAILED`, `DUPLICATE`, `DELAYED`, and `EXPIRED`.

### Out-of-Scope (Explicit Boundaries)
- Rich email template HTML drag-and-drop authoring tools.
- Real-time customer support chat messaging.
- Mobile push token generation inside client operating systems.

---

## 2. Requirements and SLAs

### Functional Requirements
1. **Multi-Channel Dispatch**: Distribute messages via the cheapest viable channel that satisfies delivery speed requirements.
2. **Priority Isolation**: High-volume marketing campaigns must never delay or starve critical security OTPs.
3. **Deduplication**: Prevent sending duplicate notifications caused by client retry storms.

### Non-Functional Requirements & SLAs
- **P0 Delivery Latency**: 99.9% of P0 messages (Two-Factor OTPs) delivered in under **5 seconds**.
- **P1 Delivery Latency**: 99.0% of P1 messages (Order confirmations) delivered in under **60 seconds**.
- **P2 Delivery Latency**: Best effort; scheduled during off-peak hours (delivery within 2 hours).
- **Throughput**: Sized for **500 Million notifications per day**.
- **System Availability**: 99.99% uptime for message ingestion.

---

## 3. Capacity Planning and Calculations

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Ingest[500M Daily Ingested<br/>Average QPS: 5,787<br/>Peak QPS: 23,148] --> Cascade[Smart Routing Cascade]
    Cascade --> Push[80% Mobile Push: 400M / Day<br/>Zero Vendor Transit Cost]
    Cascade --> Email[15% Email: 75M / Day<br/>Cost: $0.0001 / Email]
    Cascade --> SMS[5% SMS: 25M / Day<br/>Cost: $0.015 / SMS]

    classDef cStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class Ingest,Cascade,Push,Email,SMS cStyle;
```

### Ingestion Throughput Sizing
- **Daily Ingestion**: 500 Million notifications per day.
- **Average Ingestion QPS**:
  $$\text{Average QPS} = \frac{500,000,000}{86,400\text{ seconds}} \approx \mathbf{5,787\text{ notifications/sec}}$$
- **Peak Ingestion QPS (4x Multiplier for flash events)**:
  $$\text{Peak QPS} = 5,787 \times 4 \approx \mathbf{23,148\text{ notifications/sec}}$$
- **Average Ingestion Payload**: $1\text{ KB}$ (includes recipient IDs, template variables, metadata).
- **Ingestion Network Bandwidth**:
  $$\text{Bandwidth} = 23,148\text{ QPS} \times 1\text{ KB} \approx 23.1\text{ MB/s} = \mathbf{185\text{ Mbps ingress}}$$

### Storage Sizing (90-Day Operational Log Horizon)
- Daily storage for notification logs:
  $$\text{Daily Storage} = 500\text{M} \times 1\text{ KB} = 500\text{ GB/day}$$
- **90-Day Retention Storage**:
  $$\text{Storage} = 500\text{ GB/day} \times 90 \approx \mathbf{45\text{ Terabytes}}$$
- After 90 days, automated lifecycle policies compress and archive logs to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible for statutory audit retention.

### Financial Cost Optimization Modeling: SMS vs Push
- **Unoptimized Strategy (Blind SMS fallback)**:
  - If 500M messages were sent indiscriminately via SMS at $\$0.015$ per SMS:
    $$\text{Annual Cost} = 500,000,000 \times \$0.015 \times 365 = \mathbf{\$2.73\text{ Billion / Year}}$$
- **Optimized Smart-Routing Cascade**:
  - 80% delivered via Mobile Push (APNs / FCM): $400\text{M} \times \$0.0000 = \$0$.
  - 15% delivered via Email (SendGrid / SES): $75\text{M} \times \$0.0001 \times 365 = \$2.73\text{M / Year}$.
  - 5% delivered via SMS (Critical OTPs or uninstalled app): $25\text{M} \times \$0.015 \times 365 = \$136.8\text{M / Year}$.
  - **Net Annual Savings**: Over **\$2.5 Billion** in carrier messaging fees.

---

## 4. End-to-End System Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    ClientApps[Internal Services: Auth, Checkout, CRM] --> IngestGW[Notification Ingestion Gateway]
    
    IngestGW --> DedupCheck{Redis Deduplication Check}
    DedupCheck -->|Duplicate: Drop| DropLog[Record DUPLICATE State in DB]
    DedupCheck -->|New: Accept| PrefFilter[Preferences & Quiet Hours Filter]
    
    PrefFilter <--> UserPrefStore[(User Preferences: DynamoDB / Redis)]
    PrefFilter <--> DeviceTokenStore[(Device Token Registry: PostgreSQL)]
    
    PrefFilter --> PriorityRouter{Priority Topic Router}
    
    PriorityRouter -->|P0 Urgent OTP| KafkaP0[(Kafka Topic: notifications.p0)]
    PriorityRouter -->|P1 Transactional| KafkaP1[(Kafka Topic: notifications.p1)]
    PriorityRouter -->|P2 Marketing| KafkaP2[(Kafka Topic: notifications.p2)]

    KafkaP0 --> WorkerP0[High-Priority Dedicated Workers]
    KafkaP1 --> WorkerP1[Standard Workers]
    KafkaP2 --> WorkerP2[Bulk Marketing Workers]

    WorkerP0 & WorkerP1 & WorkerP2 --> Dispatcher[Channel Dispatcher & Circuit Breakers]

    Dispatcher --> APNS[Apple APNs: iOS Push]
    Dispatcher --> FCM[Google FCM: Android Push]
    Dispatcher --> SMSPrimary[Primary SMS: Twilio]
    Dispatcher --> SMSFallback[Fallback SMS: AWS SNS]
    Dispatcher --> EmailPrimary[Email: SendGrid / SES]

    APNS & FCM & SMSPrimary & SMSFallback & EmailPrimary -.-> Webhooks[Provider Delivery Webhooks]
    Webhooks --> StatusStore[(Status & Telemetry DB: ClickHouse)]

    classDef qStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef dbStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef appStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class KafkaP0,KafkaP1,KafkaP2 qStyle;
    class UserPrefStore,DeviceTokenStore,StatusStore dbStyle;
    class WorkerP0,WorkerP1,WorkerP2,Dispatcher appStyle;
```

---

## 5. API Contracts and Core Data Model

### API Contracts

#### 1. Ingest Notification
- **Endpoint**: `POST /api/v1/notifications`
- **Headers**:
  - `Content-Type: application/json`
  - `Idempotency-Key: <UUID>`
- **Request Payload**:
  ```json
  {
    "recipient_user_id": "usr_892134",
    "priority": "P0",
    "category": "AUTH_OTP",
    "template_id": "tpl_2fa_sms_01",
    "template_params": {
      "code": "849201",
      "expiry_mins": 5
    },
    "preferred_channels": ["PUSH", "SMS"]
  }
  ```
- **Response Payload (HTTP 202 Accepted)**:
  ```json
  {
    "notification_id": "notif_98712345",
    "status": "ACCEPTED",
    "recipient_user_id": "usr_892134",
    "priority": "P0",
    "enqueued_at": "2026-10-19T14:15:00Z"
  }
  ```

### Discrete Notification Lifecycle States

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ATTEMPTED: Ingestion API receives payload
    
    ATTEMPTED --> DUPLICATE: Idempotency key already processed
    DUPLICATE --> [*]
    
    ATTEMPTED --> ACCEPTED: Enqueued to Priority Kafka Topic
    
    ACCEPTED --> DELAYED: User in active Quiet Hours (P2 marketing only)
    DELAYED --> ACCEPTED: Quiet hour window expires
    
    ACCEPTED --> EXPIRED: TTL expires before worker consumes
    EXPIRED --> [*]
    
    ACCEPTED --> DELIVERED: Provider confirms delivery receipt
    DELIVERED --> [*]
    
    ACCEPTED --> FAILED: Provider returns unrecoverable error
    FAILED --> [*]
```

### Core Data Model (PostgreSQL / DynamoDB)

Table Name: `device_tokens`

| Column | Type | Constraints | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `user_id` | UUID | Foreign Key | Owner account identifier |
| `device_token` | VARCHAR(255) | **Primary Key** | APNs or FCM push token |
| `platform` | VARCHAR(10) | `IOS` or `ANDROID` | Target operating system |
| `is_active` | BOOLEAN | Default: `TRUE` | Deactivated when APNs returns `BadDeviceToken` |
| `updated_at` | TIMESTAMP | Not Null | Timestamp of last token refresh |

Table Name: `notification_events` (ClickHouse / TimescaleDB)
- **Partition Key**: `toYYYYMM(event_time)`
- **Sorting Key**: `(tenant_id, priority, status, event_time)`
- **Columns**: `notification_id`, `recipient_id`, `channel`, `provider`, `status`, `retry_count`, `latency_ms`.

---

## 6. Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) and Alternatives

### Architectural Comparison Matrix

| Criteria | Alternative 1: Single Shared Queue | Alternative 2: Priority Partitioned Kafka - Recommended | Alternative 3: AWS SQS FIFO Queues |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **P0 Starvation Risk** | High (Bulk marketing blasts block OTPs) | **Zero starvation** (Isolated worker fleets per topic) | Low (if priority queues separated) |
| **Throughput Ceiling** | Moderate (~10,000 msgs/sec) | **Extreme** (1,000,000+ msgs/sec via partitions) | Moderate (~3,000 msgs/sec batch limit) |
| **Ordering Guarantee** | Best effort | Strict chronological order per partition key | Strict total FIFO order |
| **Operational Cost** | Low | Moderate (Requires Kafka cluster maintenance) | High (Pay-per-request pricing at 500M msgs/day) |

### Decision Outcome
**Adopt Alternative 2 (Priority Partitioned Kafka Topics)**. Dedicating independent topics and worker fleets for P0, P1, and P2 guarantees that marketing campaigns never delay urgent security codes, while Kafka partition parallelism scales to peak flash sale volumes.

---

## 7. Failure-Mode and Recovery Matrix (FMEA)

| Failure Scenario | Detection Mechanism | Immediate System Behavior | Automated Recovery | Manual Runbook Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Twilio Primary SMS 5xx Outage** | Circuit Breaker trips (> 5% errors over 10s) | Worker immediately routes SMS traffic to secondary vendor (AWS SNS / Sinch) | Circuit breaker enters Half-Open state after 30s to test Twilio recovery | Check Twilio status page; notify vendor account manager |
| **APNs BadDeviceToken Error** | APNs returns HTTP 410 Gone | Worker marks notification as failed for push; falls back to SMS if P0 | Worker asynchronously updates `device_tokens` setting `is_active = FALSE` | Run weekly cron cleanup to purge tokens inactive > 90 days |
| **Redis Deduplication Cache Down** | Connection timeout to Redis cluster | System logs warning; bypasses deduplication to ensure P0 messages deliver | Redis Cluster Sentinel initiates replica failover in under 5 seconds | Verify Redis memory saturation and eviction metrics |
| **Downstream Webhook Flooding** | Provider webhook worker CPU > 85% | Ingestion rate temporarily exceeds database write capacity | Webhook receivers write directly to Kafka topic before ClickHouse ingestion | Increase webhook worker pod count via Kubernetes HPA |

---

## 8. Security, Privacy, and Regulatory Governance

1. **Quiet-Hour Enforcement**:
   - For all non-P0 marketing notifications, the engine calculates the user's local timezone.
   - If local time is between 10:00 PM and 8:00 AM, the notification transitions to `DELAYED` and is scheduled in a delay queue for 8:05 AM local delivery.
2. **PII and Financial Masking**:
   - Two-Factor OTP codes and financial account balances are omitted from persistent notification event logs. Logs store `template_id` and masked values (e.g. `******`).
3. **GDPR Right to be Forgotten**:
   - When a user deletes their account, device tokens and notification preferences are purged immediately. Historic delivery audit logs have `recipient_user_id` replaced with a cryptographic hash.

---

## 9. Observability and Monitoring Thresholds

| Metric Name | Telemetry Type | Target Baseline | P1 Critical Alert Threshold |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **P0 End-to-End Delivery Latency** | Metric (Histogram) | $< 3.0\text{ seconds}$ | $> 5.0\text{ seconds}$ for 2 consecutive minutes |
| **P0 Kafka Consumer Lag** | Metric (Gauge) | $< 100\text{ messages}$ | $> 1,000\text{ messages}$ (Triggers auto-scaling) |
| **Third-Party Circuit Breaker State** | Metric (State / Enum) | `CLOSED` | `OPEN` (Triggers Slack / PagerDuty notification) |
| **APNs/FCM Invalid Token Rate** | Metric (Counter) | $< 1.0\%$ | $> 5.0\%$ (Indicates token sync corruption) |

---

## 10. Migration, Launch Gates, and TPM Execution Plan

### Phased Migration Milestones

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M1[Milestone 1: Multi-Channel Gateway Build] --> M2[Milestone 2: Priority Routing & DLQ Testing]
    M2 --> M3[Milestone 3: 5% Canary Traffic on Marketing P2]
    M3 --> M4[Milestone 4: Cutover P1 Transactional & P0 Urgent]

    classDef mStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class M1,M2,M3,M4 mStyle;
```

### RACI Matrix

| Program Deliverable | Engineering Lead | Senior TPM | Security Architect | Vendor Lead (Twilio/SendGrid) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Smart Routing Engine** | **Accountable** | Consulted | Informed | Informed |
| **Carrier Rate Limit Procurement** | Consulted | **Accountable** | Informed | Responsible |
| **Quiet Hours & GDPR Compliance** | Responsible | **Accountable** | Consulted | Informed |
| **Vendor Contract SLAs & Credits** | Informed | **Accountable** | Informed | Responsible |

---

## 11. Practice System Design Questions and Model Answers

### Question 1: How do you prevent a marketing blast from delaying a user's critical Two-Factor Authentication (OTP)?
**Model Answer**:
We enforce strict physical and logical queue segregation. Ingestion APIs evaluate the priority tag (`P0` vs `P2`). Critical OTPs enter an isolated Kafka topic (`notifications.p0`) served by a dedicated, pre-provisioned worker fleet with low concurrency limits and strict latency SLAs. Bulk marketing enters `notifications.p2` served by an elastic worker fleet that throttles consumption based on downstream provider rate limits, guaranteeing zero resource contention.

### Question 2: If a user uninstalls the mobile app, how does the system prevent wasting resources on dead push tokens?
**Model Answer**:
When APNs or FCM attempts delivery to an uninstalled device, the provider returns an explicit HTTP 410 Gone error with error codes like `BadDeviceToken` or `NotRegistered`. The channel worker captures this response, publishes an invalidation event to `tokens.invalidated`, and updates the `device_tokens` table to set `is_active = FALSE`. Subsequent notifications for that user automatically skip the push attempt and fall back to SMS/Email, protecting our sender reputation.

---

## 12. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **Apple Push Notification Service Guide**: *Sending Notification Requests to APNs* (Apple Developer Documentation).
- **Firebase Cloud Messaging**: *FCM Architectural Overview* (Google Cloud Documentation).
- **Twilio SMS Architecture**: *Handling Rate Limits and High-Volume Messaging* (Twilio Docs).
- *Enterprise Integration Patterns* by Gregor Hohpe (Addison-Wesley, 2003) - Priority Queue Pattern.

# Case Study 3: Global Video Streaming Platform (YouTube / Netflix)

[Home](../README.md) > [Module 5: Real-World Case Studies](./README.md) > **Case Study 5.3: Video Streaming Platform**

---

## 1. Problem Statement and Scope

Video streaming platforms distribute massive multimedia files across the globe with minimal buffering, sub-second start latency, and adaptive quality. For technical program managers, this system design tests your ability to orchestrate heavy asynchronous compute pipelines, manage multi-terabit bandwidth cost structures, and deploy edge content distribution networks.

### In-Scope Functional Capabilities
- Direct video upload via pre-signed object storage URLs.
- Video chunking and distributed Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) transcoding.
- Multi-resolution encoding (360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) using H.264 and AV1 codecs.
- Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (HLS and MPEG-DASH) via master playlist manifests.
- Multi-tier edge caching with Internet Service Provider (ISP) embedded CDN appliances.

### Out-of-Scope (Explicit Boundaries)
- Live interactive streaming with low-latency WebRTC (e.g. Twitch chat/stream sync).
- Real-time video recommendation algorithms and machine learning training pipelines.
- User comments and social reaction feeds.

---

## 2. Requirements and SLAs

### Functional Requirements
1. **Video Ingestion**: Creators upload raw video files of up to 50 GB.
2. **Transcoding Pipeline**: System converts uploaded videos into multiple resolutions and 5-second chunk segments.
3. **Smooth Playback**: Client players dynamically switch video resolutions without playback interruption based on fluctuating network bandwidth.

### Non-Functional Requirements & SLAs
- **Playback Availability**: **99.99% Uptime** (Users must not experience playback failure).
- **Video Start Time (VST)**: p95 under **1,000 milliseconds**.
- **Rebuffering Ratio**: Less than **0.5%** of total playback time spent buffering.
- **Transcoding Latency**: Processing time should not exceed $1.5\times$ the raw video duration (e.g. a 60-minute video transcode completes in under 90 minutes).

---

## 3. Capacity Planning and Calculations

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Upload[Upload Rate: 500 hrs/min<br/>Daily Raw: 1.44 Petabytes] --> Transcode[Parallel DAG Transcoder Fleet<br/>Generates 3.6 PB Processed Media/Day]
    Transcode --> Stream[10M Concurrent Viewers<br/>Peak Egress Bandwidth: 30 Terabits/Sec]
    Stream --> CDN[95% Absorbed by Edge CDN & ISP Peering]

    classDef cStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    class Upload,Transcode,Stream,CDN cStyle;
```

### Video Ingestion Math (YouTube Scale)
- **Upload Rate**: **500 hours of video uploaded every minute**.
- **Daily Hours Uploaded**:
  $$\text{Daily Hours} = 500\text{ hrs/min} \times 60 \times 24 = \mathbf{720,000\text{ hours/day}}$$
- **Raw Storage Calculation**:
  - Compressed high-quality master copy ($2\text{ GB per hour}$):
    $$\text{Daily Raw Ingestion} = 720,000 \times 2\text{ GB} = \mathbf{1.44\text{ Petabytes/day}}$$
- **Transcoded Multi-Resolution Storage**:
  - Generating 360p ($0.4\text{ GB/hr}$), 720p ($1.0\text{ GB/hr}$), 1080p ($2.0\text{ GB/hr}$), and 4K ($4.0\text{ GB/hr}$) totals $\approx 7.4\text{ GB per hour}$ across all resolutions.
  - Total Daily Processed Storage: $720,000 \times 7.4\text{ GB} \approx \mathbf{5.33\text{ Petabytes/day}}$.
  - 5-Year Processed Media Storage: $5.33\text{ PB/day} \times 365 \times 5 \approx \mathbf{9.7\text{ Exabytes}}$.

### Playback Streaming Bandwidth Math
- **Active Viewers**: **100 Million Daily Active Viewers**.
- Average watch time: **30 minutes per viewer per day**.
- Average streaming bitrate across fleet: **3 Mbps** (Weighted average across 720p and 1080p).
- **Peak Concurrent Viewers**: 10% of daily active users streaming simultaneously during evening peak hours:
  $$\text{Peak Concurrent Viewers} = 100,000,000 \times 0.10 = \mathbf{10,000,000\text{ concurrent streams}}$$
- **Peak Egress Bandwidth**:
  $$\text{Peak Egress} = 10,000,000 \times 3\text{ Mbps} = 30,000,000\text{ Mbps} = \mathbf{30\text{ Terabits per second (Tbps)}}$$

### Financial Bandwidth Analysis: Why Edge CDNs and ISP Peering are Mandatory
- Standard public cloud egress (AWS CloudFront / GCP Egress) costs approximately $\$0.02$ to $\$0.05$ per GB.
- 30 Tbps streaming sustained for 4 hours of peak daily viewing generates:
  $$\text{Data Transferred} = \frac{30,000\text{ Gbps}}{8\text{ bits/byte}} \times 3,600 \times 4 \approx 54\text{ Petabytes/day}$$
- At $\$0.02$ per GB ($\$20,000$ per PB), un-peered cloud egress would cost **\$1.08 Million per day** (\$394 Million annually).
- **The Netflix Open Connect Architecture**: Deploying custom caching appliances inside local ISP datacenters offloads over **95%** of traffic, reducing public transit fees to near zero.

---

## 4. End-to-End System Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph UploadPipeline [Video Ingestion & Transcoding Pipeline]
        Creator[Content Creator] -->|1. Request Upload Session| API[API Gateway]
        API --> S3Raw[(Raw S3 Bucket: Ingestion Pool)]
        Creator -->|2. Direct Multipart Upload via Pre-signed URL| S3Raw
        S3Raw --> S3Event[S3 ObjectCreated Event]
        S3Event --> TranscodeQueue[(Transcode Job Queue: Kafka)]
        TranscodeQueue --> DAGOrch[DAG Transcoding Orchestrator]
        DAGOrch --> Splitter[Chunk Splitter: 5-Second Segments]
        Splitter --> WorkerPool[Parallel Transcoder Worker Pool: GPU Fleet]
        WorkerPool --> ManifestGen[Manifest Generator: HLS Master Playlist]
        ManifestGen --> S3Processed[(Processed Media Bucket: S3 Standard)]
    end

    subgraph PlaybackTier [Global Delivery & Edge Caching]
        Viewer[End User Video Player] -->|1. Fetch Master Playlist .m3u8| API
        Viewer -->|2. Stream Video Chunks .ts| EdgeCDN[Global CDN POPs]
        EdgeCDN -->|Cache Miss| OpenConnect[Embedded ISP Cache Appliances]
        OpenConnect -->|Cold Miss| OriginShield[Origin Shield CDN]
        OriginShield --> S3Processed
    end

    classDef pipeStyle fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef storeStyle fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef edgeStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class UploadPipeline,PlaybackTier pipeStyle;
    class S3Raw,S3Processed storeStyle;
    class EdgeCDN,OpenConnect,OriginShield edgeStyle;
```

---

## 5. API Contracts and Core Data Model

### API Contracts

#### 1. Initiate Upload Session
- **Endpoint**: `POST /api/v1/videos/upload-session`
- **Request Payload**:
  ```json
  {
    "creator_id": "usr_98124",
    "title": "Distributed Systems Handbook Walkthrough",
    "file_size_bytes": 4294967296,
    "file_format": "mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 3600
  }
  ```
- **Response Payload (HTTP 200 OK)**:
  ```json
  {
    "video_id": "vid_87213459",
    "upload_session_id": "sess_009988",
    "upload_url": "https://ingest.storage.com/raw/vid_87213459.mp4?X-Amz-Signature=...",
    "chunk_size_bytes": 10485760,
    "expires_at": "2026-10-19T18:00:00Z"
  }
  ```

#### 2. Fetch Master Playlist Manifest
- **Endpoint**: `GET /api/v1/videos/{video_id}/master.m3u8`
- **Response (HTTP 200 OK)**:
  ```m3u8
  #EXTM3U
  #EXT-X-VERSION:6
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360,CODECS="avc1.4d401e,mp4a.40.2"
  360p/index.m3u8
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2500000,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2"
  720p/index.m3u8
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2"
  1080p/index.m3u8
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=15000000,RESOLUTION=3840x2160,CODECS="av01.0.12M.08,mp4a.40.2"
  4k/index.m3u8
  ```

### Core Data Model (PostgreSQL / DynamoDB)

Table Name: `videos`
- **PK**: `video_id` (UUID)
- **Attributes**: `creator_id`, `title`, `duration_seconds`, `status` (`UPLOADING`, `TRANSCODING`, `READY`, `FAILED`), `manifest_url`, `created_at`.

Table Name: `transcoding_tasks`
- **PK**: `task_id` (UUID)
- **GSI**: `video_id`
- **Attributes**: `video_id`, `chunk_index`, `resolution`, `codec`, `status` (`PENDING`, `IN_PROGRESS`, `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`), `retry_count`, `worker_host`.

---

## 6. Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) and Alternatives

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Raw[Raw 4K Video File] --> Splitter[Chunk Splitter: 5-Second Segments]
    
    Splitter --> C1[Chunk 1: 0-5s]
    Splitter --> C2[Chunk 2: 5-10s]
    Splitter --> CN[Chunk N: 3595-3600s]

    C1 --> W1[GPU Worker 1: Transcode 360p, 720p, 1080p]
    C2 --> W2[GPU Worker 2: Transcode 360p, 720p, 1080p]
    CN --> WN[GPU Worker N: Transcode 360p, 720p, 1080p]

    W1 & W2 & WN --> Stitch[Stitch Manifest: master.m3u8]

    classDef splitStyle fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:1px;
    class Splitter,Stitch splitStyle;
```

### Architectural Comparison Matrix

| Criteria | Alternative 1: Monolithic Transcoding | Alternative 2: Chunk-Based DAG Transcoding - Recommended |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transcoding Latency** | Slow (A 2-hour 4K movie takes 3+ hours on a single machine) | **Ultra-fast** (Hundreds of workers process chunks in parallel in 5 mins) |
| **Worker Failure Blast Radius** | High (Worker crash at 99% forces full re-transcode of 2-hour file) | **Minimal** (Only the specific 5-second chunk is retried) |
| **Fast Seeking Support** | Difficult (Requires range-header parsing on monolithic file) | **Native** (Player simply fetches chunk corresponding to target timestamp) |
| **Compute Cost Profile** | Poor hardware utilization | High GPU efficiency through elastic batch worker fleets |

### Decision Outcome
**Adopt Alternative 2 (Chunk-Based DAG Transcoding)**. Splitting videos into discrete 5-second chunks parallelizes transcoding, isolates worker crashes, and supports seamless Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (HLS/DASH).

---

## 7. Failure-Mode and Recovery Matrix (FMEA)

| Failure Scenario | Detection Mechanism | Immediate System Behavior | Automated Recovery | Manual Runbook Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transcoding GPU Worker Crashes** | Worker heartbeat timeout (> 15s) in DAG engine | Chunk status reverts from `IN_PROGRESS` to `PENDING` | Orchestrator reassigns chunk to alternative healthy GPU worker | If worker fleet crashes repeatedly, check for corrupted source video chunks |
| **Edge CDN POP Outage** | Synthetic latency probes fail from geographic region | Anycast BGP border routers withdraw route to impaired POP | Traffic automatically re-routes to nearest adjacent regional CDN POP | Open P1 ticket with CDN provider (Cloudflare / Fastly) |
| **Manifest Generation Corruption** | Validation worker verifies playlist syntax | Video status marked `FAILED_VALIDATION` before public indexing | Orchestrator re-runs manifest compilation step | Inspect manifest generator logs for missing chunk indices |
| **Storage Class Cost Overrun** | Monthly AWS S3 Cost Allocation Tag alarm | Budget alert triggered when storage exceeds monthly forecast | S3 Lifecycle policy automatically moves videos $> 30$ days old to S3 Infrequent Access | Audit video watch count metrics; adjust lifecycle transition windows |

---

## 8. Security, DRM, and Content Protection

1. **Digital Rights Management (DRM)**:
   - Video chunks are encrypted using AES-128 encryption.
   - Master playlist manifests deliver encryption key URIs guarded by DRM license servers (Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine, Microsoft PlayReady).
2. **Copyright & Content ID Fingerprinting**:
   - During chunking, an asynchronous worker extracts acoustic and visual perceptual hashes, comparing them against the global copyright registry before activating the public video link.
3. **Geo-Fencing and Signed Cookies**:
   - Streaming URLs are signed with short-lived HMAC tokens (15-minute expiration) and validated against client geographic location to enforce regional licensing boundaries.

---

## 9. Observability and Monitoring Thresholds

| Metric Name | Telemetry Type | Target Baseline | P1 Critical Alert Threshold |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Video Start Time (VST)** | Metric (Histogram) | $< 1,000\text{ms}$ | $> 2,500\text{ms}$ for 5 consecutive minutes |
| **Rebuffering Ratio** | Metric (Gauge) | $< 0.5\%$ | $> 1.5\%$ (Indicates widespread edge congestion) |
| **CDN Cache Hit Ratio (CHR)** | Metric (Gauge) | $> 95\%$ | $< 85\%$ (Causes origin egress cost spike) |
| **Transcoder Queue Lag** | Metric (Gauge) | $< 500\text{ chunks}$ | $> 10,000\text{ chunks}$ (Triggers GPU cluster auto-scale) |

---

## 10. Migration, Launch Gates, and TPM Execution Plan

### Phased Migration Milestones

    T2 --> T3[Milestone 3: 5% Canary Traffic on Low-Resolution Variants]
    T3 --> T4[Milestone 4: Full Multi-Bitrate Edge Cutover with DRM]

### RACI Matrix

---

## 11. Practice System Design Questions and Model Answers

### Question 1: How does Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (HLS) dynamically adjust resolution during a network drop?
**Model Answer**:
The client video player continuously measures the download duration and byte count of incoming 5-second video chunks. When a user enters poor cell coverage, the player calculates that chunk download time has exceeded playback buffer duration. The player reads the master playlist manifest (`master.m3u8`) and automatically requests the next chunk from the lower bitrate variant (e.g. dropping from `1080p/chunk_42.ts` to `360p/chunk_43.ts`). Because chunks are aligned at identical Key Frame (I-frame) intervals, the transition is seamless and prevents rebuffering.

### Question 2: How do you prevent long-tail videos from driving cloud storage bills into insolvency?
**Model Answer**:
We implement a tiered encoding and storage lifecycle strategy. Less than 20% of uploaded videos receive sustained views after 30 days. We encode newly uploaded videos in 360p and 720p immediately; 4K encoding is deferred until a video crosses 1,000 views within 24 hours. Furthermore, automated S3 Lifecycle policies transition raw source videos to S3 Glacier after 7 days, and move transcoded chunks with zero monthly views to S3 Infrequent Access or Archive Instant Access, slashing storage costs by 60% to 75%.

---

## 12. Primary Sources and Further Reading

- **Adaptive Streaming Protocol**: RFC 8216 - HTTP Live Streaming (Apple / IETF).
- **Netflix Open Connect Architecture**: *Open Connect Deployment Guide* (Netflix Partner Documentation).
- **Distributed Video Transcoding**: *Scaling Video Transcoding at YouTube* (Google Engineering Technical Presentation).
- **MPEG-DASH Specification**: ISO/IEC 23009-1: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP.
